item.title: Kakao Pay and Toss balance limits could rise to 5 million won under a Korean plan, with no start date
item.description:
The 2 million won wall

Say you need to pay 3.5 million won, about $2,600, for flights and a hotel. A Korean pay-app wallet such as Kakao Pay, Toss or Naver Pay can hold at most 2 million won, about $1,500, even for users whose identity has been checked, so the rest has to come from a fresh top-up, a card or a bank transfer. The cap is written into the enforcement decree of the Electronic Financial Transactions Act. Dollar figures here use about 1,340 won to the dollar.

On Nov. 26 the Financial Services Commission (FSC), South Korea's main financial regulator, announced a plan to change that. Users verified through a linked bank account would be able to hold 3 million won, about $2,200, and those who pass a full real-name check 5 million won, about $3,700. The 5 million won tier would be open only at firms that pass a security review by the Financial Security Institute, the financial sector's security agency. Anonymous wallets would stay at 500,000 won, about $370.

This is general information about how the system works, not legal or financial advice.

A cap frozen since 2008

The 2 million won limit was set in July 2008. When the law took effect in January 2007, the cap was 500,000 won; only ID-verified (named) wallets were raised to 2 million the next year. According to the FSC's plan, the consumer price index rose 45.9% between July 2008, when it stood at 82.7, and October 2026, when it hit 120.7.

Adjusted for that, 2 million won in July 2008 equals about 2.92 million won today, by HOLT's calculation. By that measure the bank-linked tier of 3 million roughly keeps pace with inflation, and the real increase is the 5 million tier. The FSC cited changing spending habits as well as prices.

Usage has grown too. Average daily usage of prepaid instruments rose from 467.6 billion won in 2020 to about 1.31 trillion won in 2025, roughly $350 million to $970 million, up 179%. Tourism is part of the story. Korea passed 20 million foreign visitors for the year on Nov. 12 for the first time.

The plan would lift the cap on tourist wallets from 1 million won to 3 million, with a daily limit of 6 million won. The tourist tier comes with strings. It depends on a new ID check using e-passports, links to passport and immigration records, and a live face scan, offered only by firms that pass a security review. Spending would be limited to Korean merchants, with no transfers between users and no use 90 days after issue or once the visitor leaves the country.

A new daily limit

The plan also adds a second limit. Today only the stored balance is capped; the rules do not limit how much passes through a wallet in a day. The plan sets a daily limit covering payments, peer-to-peer transfers and similar uses of 6 million won, about $4,500, for bank-linked users and 10 million won, about $7,400, for fully verified ones.

Take the 3.5 million won trip. Today a single wallet payment tops out at 2 million won, so the other 1.5 million has to come from another top-up, a card or a transfer. A bank-linked user under the new rules would be 500,000 won short; a fully verified user at a firm cleared for the higher tier could pay it all at once.

The press release calls this a daily usage limit, while the summary table in the same plan labels it daily top-up volume. The draft rules will settle what it counts. If it counts daily spending, someone who now moves more than 6 million won (bank-linked) or 10 million won (fully verified) a day through a wallet could hit it. The FSC said firms would be guided to let users set their own per-transaction and daily limits within the legal ceiling.

When it starts

There is no date. The FSC said it would draft amendments in the first half of 2027 for items that need rule changes, which would include the caps, since they sit in the decree.

Some firms may move sooner. The FSC said that, after consulting other ministries, it would seek to raise caps before the rules change by designating services under its regulatory sandbox, with the same conditions, such as daily limits, that the final rules would impose. It has not said which firms or when.

Changes that need no rule amendment are due in the first half of 2027. The FSC will urge firms to drop large minimum top-ups such as 10,000 won, which push users to load more than they need. It will also ask them to block gambling payments, as card issuers must, and to run a round-the-clock channel for reporting account takeovers.

What protects a bigger balance

If a pay firm fails, Article 25-2 of the Electronic Financial Transactions Act requires it to keep customer balances separate, through a trust or deposit with a bank or similar institution, or through payment guarantee insurance. The law sets a floor of 50%, and Article 13-2 of the decree raises it to 100%. Money held this way cannot be seized or set off against the firm's debts.

If the firm's registration is cancelled or it goes bankrupt, the institution holding the money must pay users first when they claim it. The rule was written into the law in September 2023 and took effect a year later, in September 2024. A higher cap means more money sits under that protection.

Account takeover is a different risk. Separate custody protects users if the firm fails, not if someone empties their account, and a bigger balance means more can leave at once. The plan presents usage limits as a way to curb misuse of prepaid wallets; for users it would also cap how much a taken-over wallet could lose in a day.

The plan would also require identity checks when an access credential, the password, card or certificate used to reach an account, is issued for a named prepaid wallet, and would restrict handing one over. For other financial accounts, transferring or trading an access credential already carries up to five years in prison or a fine of up to 30 million won, about $22,000. Prepaid wallets are outside the transfer ban, though lending one knowing it will be used for crime is already punishable.

item.title: Seoul apartment gifts surged in the month before two Korean tax changes
item.description:
Incentives

One of the first principles in any economics textbook is that people respond to incentives, the rewards and penalties that make an action more or less attractive. When a price rises, people buy less. When a deadline approaches, they hurry.

This builds on the last chapter. People weigh what one more step gains against what it costs, and when a government changes that cost through a tax or a rule, choices shift with it. If a change is known in advance, some people move before it takes effect.

1,000 gifted apartments in one month

According to the Korea Real Estate Board, a state-run agency that tracks property deals, 1,000 Seoul apartments changed owners as gifts in December 2022. In the same month, 1,001 were sold. Gifts and sales were nearly level. A month earlier, in November, there had been 305 gifts; a month later, in January 2023, there were 489. Dollar figures below use 1,340 won to the dollar.

The calendar is the likely explanation. Anyone who receives a home in South Korea owes acquisition tax, a local tax paid by the new owner, including when the home is a gift. It is separate from Korea's gift tax, which is also paid by the person receiving the gift, not the giver as in the United States. An amendment to the Local Tax Act, promulgated on December 28, 2021, changed how acquisition tax on gifts is calculated from January 1, 2023. Before, the tax was based on the value the taxpayer declared, but never less than the government's official assessed price, a figure set each year mainly for property taxes, which for many homes sits below the market. In practice that allowed a gift to be declared at the assessed price. From 2023 it is applied to a market-based value: recent sale prices of similar units, an appraisal or an auction price. For a home assessed below its market price, waiting until January meant a bigger bill. The rules treat a gift as acquired on the date of the gift contract, so a contract signed in December still fell under the old rule.

The statistics may record a different month from the one in which the contract was signed. Nor do the figures explain why Seoul gifts jumped again to 1,420 in February 2023. Inherited homes are still taxed on the assessed price, and for homes assessed at 100 million won or less, the taxpayer may choose either figure. If a market-based value cannot be set, the assessed price is used.

A 10.5 million won difference

Take an apartment with an assessed price of 700 million won, about $522,000, and a market price of 1 billion won, about $746,000, given to a child by a parent whose household owns only that home, so the surcharge does not apply and the standard 3.5% rate does. The figures count only the acquisition tax itself, leaving out the smaller surtaxes and the separate gift tax.

A gift contract signed in December 2022 was taxed at 3.5% of 700 million won: 24.5 million won, about $18,300. One signed in January 2023, with the 1 billion won market price accepted as the value, was taxed at 35 million won, about $26,100. One month apart, the gap was 10.5 million won, about $7,800. Had no exception applied and the 12% rate been due, the bills would have been 84 million won, about $62,700, and 120 million won, about $89,600, a gap of 36 million won, about $26,900. The 12% rate applies only if the home is in a regulated area when the contract is signed, and those designations are sometimes lifted.

This is general information, not tax, legal or financial advice. Actual bills can be checked with the local district office or Korea's online local tax service, Wetax.

July 2020: 3,362 gifts

In 2020 it was the rate that changed. A Local Tax Act amendment that took effect on August 12, 2020, the day it was promulgated, raised the acquisition tax on gifts of homes with an assessed value of 300 million won or more, about $224,000, in regulated areas, from 3.5% to 12%. Regulated areas are the hot housing markets where the government applies tighter rules. Homes of a household that owns only one home, passed to a spouse or another direct-line relative such as a child or parent, were among the exceptions. For a home assessed at 700 million won, the tax went from 24.5 million won to 84 million won, a difference of 59.5 million won, about $44,400. The amendment took effect the day it was promulgated, so there was no preset date; whether the July rise reflected policy plans known beforehand, the statistics cannot say.

In July, the last month before the change, gifts of Seoul apartments reached 3,362, 2.3 times June's 1,473. They did not drop once the change took effect. There were 2,768 in August, 2,843 in September, 1,744 in October and 2,400 in November. Every month from August to December 2020 stayed above 1,700, against a 2019 monthly average of 1,043. December 2022 looked different: gifts fell to 489 in January, but only for a month, rising to 1,420 in February. Over the year, Seoul apartment gifts rose from 12,514 in 2019 to 23,675 in 2020, 1.9 times as many.

Another incentive moved at the same time. An Income Tax Act amendment, promulgated on August 18, 2020, raised the surcharge on capital gains for owners of several homes in regulated areas, from June 1, 2021. For a second home it went from 10 to 20 percentage points on top of the normal rate, and for a third or more from 20 to 30 points. That is a different tax under a different law. The statistics cannot separate how much of the 2020 rise came from the gift tax deadline, how much from the coming surcharge on sales, and how much from neither. In 2021, the year the surcharge began, gifts of Seoul apartments fell back to 12,435, about the 2019 level.

A share depends on the total

A share can mislead. Gifts made up 4.0% of Seoul apartment transfers in 2016, 14.2% in 2020 and 14.1% in 2022. But only 15,384 Seoul apartments were sold in 2022, about a sixth of 2020's 93,784. Gifts that year numbered 5,791, a quarter of 2020's, yet their share stayed high because total transfers fell even further, from 166,847 in 2020 to 41,207 in 2022.

It works the other way too. After gifts began to be taxed on market value, their share fell to 7.9% in 2023 and 5.9% in 2025. The number of gifts did not fall: 6,610 in 2023 and 6,863 in 2025, more than in 2022. Much of the drop in share came from total transfers doubling, from 41,207 in 2022 to 83,922 in 2023. A rule change shows up sharply right before a deadline, but over the following years its effect is hard to separate from the rest of the market.

Reading the news with incentives in mind

When a story says deals suddenly surged or dried up, it helps to look for a rule that changed around then and the date it took effect. Then separate counts from shares, and check whether the surge stopped at the deadline or carried on. That gets you a little closer to telling what a policy changed from what other forces changed.

The next chapter covers gains from trade and comparative advantage: why two people or two countries that are good at different things can both come out ahead by trading, told through trade figures.

item.title: Don't itemize? You can still deduct up to $1,000 in cash gifts for 2026
item.description:
What changed for 2026?

A cash gift to charity can now lower your federal income tax even if you don't itemize. For tax years 2022 through 2025, people who took the standard deduction got nothing from such a gift; a temporary $300 version ($600 for joint filers) applied only to 2021. That changes with gifts made in 2026. Under the tax law Congress passed in July 2025, which the IRS calls the Working Families Tax Cuts, people who do not itemize can deduct up to $1,000 of cash donations to qualified charities, or $2,000 for married couples filing jointly. The $1,000 limit applies to every other filing status, including heads of household and each spouse who files separately. The deduction is permanent, and it comes on top of the 2026 standard deduction of $16,100 for single filers and $32,200 for joint filers.

The IRS reminded taxpayers of the rule on Nov. 10, ahead of the 2027 filing season, when 2026 returns are due. Only gifts made by Dec. 31, 2026 count toward this year's return. A gift charged to a credit card counts in the year the charge is made, according to IRS Publication 526.

This is general information, not tax, legal or financial advice. The IRS rules and publications linked below are the reference for any individual situation.

How much does it actually save?

The deduction lowers the income you are taxed on, so the tax saved is the deductible amount times your marginal rate, the rate on your last dollars of income. The saving applies only if you owe federal income tax to begin with. For 2026, the 12% bracket covers taxable income up to $50,400 for single filers and $100,800 for joint filers, and the 22% bracket runs up to $105,700 and $211,400.

For a single filer whose taxable income is $60,000, in the 22% bracket, a $1,000 cash gift cuts federal income tax by $220. A single filer in the 12% bracket who gives $600 saves $72. For a married couple filing jointly, a $2,000 gift saves $240 in the 12% bracket and $440 in the 22% bracket. If the same couple gives $3,000, only $2,000 counts, so the saving stays at $440 and the extra $1,000 earns nothing under this rule.

The calculator below repeats the math: enter the part of your gift that counts, up to $1,000 or $2,000, and your bracket rate. It leaves out state income tax; whether a state follows this federal deduction depends on that state's own rules.

Which gifts don't count?

Only cash gifts qualify, and cash here includes checks, card payments and bank transfers. Clothing, household goods and stock do not count toward this deduction. Neither do gifts to donor-advised funds, accounts held by a sponsoring charity so donors can recommend grants to other charities later, or to supporting organizations, charities that exist to support other public charities.

The money also has to go to a public charity of the kind the law lists in section 170(b)(1)(A). Gifts to individuals or political groups are not deductible. The IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search tool shows a deductibility code for each listed group: codes such as 50% (60% for cash), PC, POF or FED generally qualify, while any other code, including that of a private non-operating foundation, means extra rules apply and the gift may not count here. Some churches and government bodies are not listed separately and can still qualify.

Publication 526 (2025 edition, the latest available) sets the record rules: a bank record or a receipt showing the charity's name, the date and the amount, and for any single gift of $250 or more, the charity's written acknowledgment, obtained by the earlier of the filing date or the due date including extensions. A benefit dinner is not all gift: only the part above the value of what you receive is deductible, and raffle tickets are not deductible at all.

What changes for people who itemize?

Itemizers face a new hurdle. Starting in 2026, they can deduct charitable gifts only to the extent the year's total, cash or not, exceeds 0.5% of their contribution base, which for most people is AGI. A couple with $150,000 of adjusted gross income cannot deduct the first $750 of their gifts that year. The law spares the non-itemizer deduction from this floor, so someone who does not itemize keeps the full $1,000 or $2,000.

Consider that couple, and assume their only other itemized deductions are $25,000 of state and local taxes and mortgage interest. If they give $5,000, itemizing would give them $29,250 in deductions: $25,000 plus $4,250 of gifts after the floor. Taking the standard deduction plus the $2,000 charity deduction gives $34,200. The standard route is bigger, and the gift saves them $440 compared with giving nothing.

If the couple gives $12,000 instead, itemizing reaches $36,250, which beats $34,200, and the gift lowers their tax by $891 at 22% compared with giving nothing. For this couple the break-even is $9,950: for gifts from $2,000 up to that amount, the standard deduction plus the $2,000 charity deduction comes out ahead. A couple with a different income or other deductions has a different break-even, found the same way.

At the top of the income scale there is a second limit. For filers in the 37% bracket, which starts at $640,600 of taxable income for single filers and $768,700 for joint filers in 2026, the law cuts itemized deductions of all kinds, not just charity, by 2/37 of the smaller of the total itemized deductions or the amount by which taxable income before this limit, with those deductions added back, exceeds that threshold. When every one of them sits inside the top bracket, each dollar saves 35 cents instead of 37. The non-itemizer deduction is not affected.

What could still trip you up?

Does the date matter? Yes. Publication 526 says a check counts as given on the day you mail it, so a check mailed on Dec. 31 belongs to 2026. A gift made on Jan. 2, 2027 belongs to the 2027 tax year.

The IRS says the deduction goes only to people who do not itemize, so a household cannot take both this deduction and itemized charitable deductions on the same return. You do not have to take the standard deduction to qualify, IRS Publication 6196 notes: someone who cannot take it, such as a married person filing separately whose spouse itemizes, can still claim the charity deduction as long as they do not itemize. The IRS also notes that carryovers from prior years do not qualify for this deduction.

item.title: 6.5 million UK mortgages are projected to pay more by 2029, Bank of England says
item.description:
6.5 million mortgages by the end of 2029

About 7 million of the UK's roughly 9 million owner-occupier mortgages are projected to refinance between June 2026 and December 2029, the Bank of England said in its Financial Stability Report on Nov. 26. It expects payments to rise on about 6.5 million of them, up from about 6 million in its July report, and to fall on about 350,000. Fixed-rate deals ending drive the estimate; variable-rate loans are counted too. Buy-to-let mortgages and loans under £1,000 are excluded.

For a typical owner-occupier coming off a fixed deal in the next three years, the Bank projects a median rise in monthly repayments of about £100, roughly $131. That is about twice the July estimate, though still well below the median rise of just under £200 for borrowers who remortgaged in 2023 and 2024. The vast majority of the 6.5 million have already moved at least once onto rates well above those available before 2022, the Bank said.

The projection assumes borrowers move onto rates implied by market pricing, the overnight index swap curve, as of Nov. 18. General information, not tax, legal or financial advice. Actual rates and payments depend on each loan and lender.

Deals fixed before 2022 face bigger jumps

British borrowers on a fixed rate move onto a new deal when it ends, so a rise in rates tends to arrive all at once, on the day the old deal ends. The Bank's database shows the average quoted 5-year fixed rate at 75% loan to value ranged from 1.28% to 1.92% in month-end readings through 2021, and stood at 1.52% in November 2021. At the end of October 2026 it was 5.19%, the highest since September 2023 (5.24%). Since the end of July, quoted 2-year fixes have gone from 4.79% to 5.39% and 5-year fixes from 4.58% to 5.19%.

As an illustration, not a case the Bank cited: take a £200,000 repayment mortgage over 25 years, fixed at 1.52% for five years in November 2021. The monthly payment is £801.75. Five years later the balance is £165,835. Refixed at 5.19% for the remaining 20 years, the payment becomes £1,111.92, about £310, or $406, more a month, a 39% rise in the monthly bill. The calculator below takes your own numbers.

Just over 1 million households on mortgage rates below 3% are due to refinance by the fourth quarter of 2027, the Bank said. By then most mortgages still on such low rates will have refinanced.

Arrears are still near normal

The pressure has not yet shown up as a sharp rise in missed payments. About 0.8% of mortgages have more than 2.5% of their balance in arrears, the Bank said, close to the long-run average. Household debt is about 130% of income, below the post-2000 average of 153%, and households hold cash worth about 140% of income. Debt-servicing burdens, though, are back around their long-run averages and projected to rise. The Bank cautioned that arrears figures look backward and may not yet capture recent rate increases.

The same report shows major UK banks returned £9.2 billion to shareholders through buybacks and dividends in the third quarter. Separately, the Financial Policy Committee said its proposals would cut big banks' Tier 1 capital requirements, the core capital they must hold, by about 0.5 percentage point of risk-weighted assets in normal times, freeing up capacity to lend. Its record also restates the guidance that loans at 4.5 times income or more should make up no more than 15% of new mortgages.

Korea's new loans mostly float

South Korea's mortgage market is built differently. Bank of Korea data show that by value, 38.1% of new bank mortgages in October carried a fixed rate and 61.9% a variable one. Across all outstanding bank mortgages, 60.5% are fixed.

Korean variable-rate home loans typically reset on dates set in the contract, tracking a benchmark such as COFIX, a bank funding-cost index. The Bank of Korea raised its policy rate to 3.25% on Nov. 26; as that feeds into the benchmark, variable-rate borrowers see the change at their next reset. In Britain, where Bank Rate went up to 4% on Nov. 5, rate rises reach households when fixed deals end; Korean variable-rate borrowers see them in steps at each reset.

What could change the numbers

The 6.5 million and £100 figures assume fixed-rate borrowers refinance at the typical rate the swap curve implies when their deal ends, and that variable-rate payments move with the same curve. Lower market rates would shrink the increases; higher ones would enlarge them.

In the Bank's adverse scenario, a more prolonged energy shock, households' debt payments plus essential spending as a share of income would rise to close to 16%, the highest since the global financial crisis but about 2.5 percentage points below its peak then. The rates locked in by the low-rate borrowers who remortgage before the end of 2027 could matter most for how the 6.5 million and £100 estimates turn out.

item.title: Korea health insurance cost vs. the US: what workers and patients pay
item.description:
The short answer

South Korea has one public health insurer for almost everyone: the National Health Insurance Service. Employees are enrolled through work. The self-employed and retirees pay on their own, with premiums based on income and property rather than a flat share of wages. A worker's spouse, children and parents can be covered as dependents if they mainly rely on the worker for a living and their income and assets are under limits set by the health ministry. Coverage is universal and there is a single public payer, so there is no choice of plan and no network. The same coverage works at almost any clinic or hospital in the country.

Coverage is not free at the point of care. The patient pays part of every covered bill, and some services are not covered at all. Behind that is a yearly cap, set by premium bracket, on what a patient pays for covered care. In short, most employees pay about 3.6% of pay for health insurance, plus a little under 0.5% for long-term care, and adults usually pay 30% of a covered clinic bill.

What a worker pays each month

In 2026 the premium rate is 7.19% of wages, up from 7.09% in 2025. A long-term care premium, which funds a separate public program for frail older people, is added on top at 0.9448% of income. For most employees, the worker pays half and the employer pays the other half. This covers wages only. Large income outside a job can add a separate premium that the worker pays alone.

Take a worker earning 4 million won a month, about $2,975 at 1,344.5 won to the dollar, the rate on Nov. 26. The worker's share is 143,800 won for health insurance and about 18,900 won for long-term care, about 162,700 won a month in all, or about $121. Over a year that comes to about 1.95 million won, or $1,452. The base is the pay counted for premiums under the act. The employer pays the same amount again, so the combined premium for this worker's household is about $2,904 a year.

That amount does not change if the worker adds a spouse or two children who qualify as dependents. In the US, KFF's 2025 survey of employer plans found an average family premium of $26,993, of which workers paid $6,850 out of their paychecks. The two figures are not like for like. Korea's premium rises and falls with pay, the insurer also receives a government contribution that the law calls for at 14% of expected premium income under Article 108-2 of the act, the 4 million won salary is an example rather than a Korean average, and the US number is an average family plan price before deductibles and copays. Read them as a sense of scale, not a ranking.

What a patient pays at the clinic or hospital

Korea sorts providers by size: clinics, hospitals, general hospitals with many specialties, and top-tier hospitals. It sets the patient's share by law, not by plan. For most adults, a covered outpatient visit in a city costs the patient 30% at a neighborhood clinic, 40% at a hospital and 50% at a general hospital. At a top-tier hospital, usually a large university hospital, the bill is the full exam fee plus 60% of the rest. In eup and myeon areas outside cities, general hospitals and hospitals charge 5 points less. Pregnant women, babies under 1 and older patients with small bills follow different rules.

So for every 10,000 won (about $7.44) of covered care at a neighborhood clinic, the patient pays 3,000 won, about $2.23. There is no deductible to meet first. For a stay in a standard ward, the patient pays 20% of covered costs and half of the meal charges. Rooms with fewer beds cost more, 30% to 50% of the room charge. Patients registered with an illness on the health ministry's serious-illness list pay 5% for care tied to that illness.

In the US, KFF found the average deductible for single coverage, among workers with a general annual deductible, was $1,886 in 2025, and 29% of covered workers were in high-deductible plans that qualify for a health savings account. Copays and coinsurance then vary by plan and network. Korea has one national benefit design, so the shares above apply nationwide.

The yearly cap, and what it leaves out

Korea limits how much a patient pays in a year for covered care. The decree set seven brackets for 2024, based on the premium a person pays, which tracks income, with caps from 870,000 won for the lowest bracket to 8.08 million won for the highest. From 2025 each cap rises with the previous year's inflation rate, and amounts under 10,000 won are dropped. Official consumer prices rose 2.3% in 2024 and 2.1% in 2025. Applying the decree's formula, HOLT NEWS's calculation puts the 2026 caps at 900,000 won to 8.43 million won, about $669 to $6,270. Long stays in long-term care hospitals have higher caps. When a patient's covered payments pass the cap, the insurer pays the rest or refunds it later. The National Health Insurance Service notice is the final word on each bracket.

The cap counts only the patient's share of covered care. Uncovered services, called bigeubyeo in Korean, are billed in full and do not count toward it. Some upgraded hospital rooms, many cosmetic procedures and certain tests and treatments the health ministry has not listed fall in this group, and they can add up to large bills. Private supplemental insurance, called silson in Korean, can cover part of them.

What this means for Americans in Korea

Foreign residents who work for a Korean employer and have registered as foreigners generally join the system as employees under Article 109 of the act, with some exceptions, and pay the same rates. Foreigners who are not on a Korean payroll can enroll on their own if they meet the residence period and visa categories set by the health ministry, and their premiums can be set differently from those for employees.

The numbers in this article are the 2026 rates and the decree as amended on Sept. 15, 2026, in force since Oct. 1. Premium rates are set each year, and the National Health Insurance Service posts each year's rate on its English site.

General information about Korea's system, not medical, insurance or financial advice.

item.title: Bank of Korea raises its policy rate to 3.25%, the third hike since July
item.description:
Three hikes since July

The Bank of Korea raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 3.25% on Nov. 26. It is the third increase this year, after moves to 2.75% on July 16 and 3.00% on Aug. 27. The rate stood at 2.50% through June, so it has risen 0.75 percentage points since mid-July.

Five of the seven members of the Monetary Policy Board backed the hike. Hwang Kun-il and Lee Soo-hyung wanted to hold at 3.00%. The statement cited stronger growth and inflation expected to stay above the 2% target for a considerable period, and flagged financial-stability risks from Seoul-area housing and household debt. The bank raised its growth forecast for this year and next to 3.9% and 4.1%, up from 3.3% and 2.9% in August. Consumer prices rose 2.8% from a year earlier in October.

The statement's closing line says the board will decide the timing of additional hikes. The wording leaves the timing open; it does not rule more increases out.

New loans rose more

Lending rates did not wait for the meeting. Bank of Korea data show the average rate on new variable-rate mortgages at deposit banks was 4.90% in October, up 0.63 points from 4.27% in June. Over the same period the policy rate rose 0.50 points. Rates on new unsecured personal loans rose 0.71 points, from 5.72% to 6.43%. The CD rate rose 0.34 points over the same period, so bank margins and other factors may also be at work.

The 91-day certificate of deposit rate, a benchmark for bank loan pricing, averaged 2.91% in June and 3.25% in October, already at the new policy rate. COFIX, the cost-of-funds index published by the Korea Federation of Banks and widely used as a benchmark for variable-rate mortgages, was 3.62% for new funds in October.

Existing borrowers are a different story. The average rate on all outstanding variable-rate mortgages rose only 0.23 points, from 4.28% to 4.51%. Korean variable-rate loans reset on dates set in the loan contract, often every few months to a year, so higher benchmarks reach existing borrowers one reset at a time.

When a borrower feels it

A Korean variable rate is a benchmark plus a margin set when the loan was signed. The benchmark (COFIX, the CD rate or a bank bond yield) and the reset schedule differ by loan. Both appear in the loan agreement and usually in the bank's app.

For a loan that resets every six months on new-funds COFIX, the figure published just before the reset date sets the new rate. November COFIX comes out on Dec. 15. It covers bank funding costs for the whole month, so it includes only five days after the hike; December and later readings will show more.

Hybrid loans, which are fixed for a few years and then float, follow the same rules once the fixed period ends. Fixed-rate loans are unaffected for their fixed term.

What a quarter point costs

Take a 300 million won ($223,000) mortgage repaid in equal monthly installments over 30 years. If its rate rises from 4.90% to 5.15%, the payment goes from 1,592,180 won to 1,638,079 won, up 45,899 won ($34) a month, or 550,782 won a year.

On an interest-only loan the math is simpler: 300 million won times 0.25% is 750,000 won a year, or 62,500 won a month. On a 50 million won personal loan repaid at maturity, monthly interest rises by 10,417 won.

What a borrower actually pays depends on where the benchmark sits on the reset date, which may be more or less than a quarter point higher. For scale, if a borrower's rate rose as much as the average new-loan rate did, from 4.27% to 4.90%, the payment on a 30-year, 300 million won loan would rise by 112,846 won a month. The calculator below works with any amount and rate.

Fixed rates and early repayment fees

In October, new fixed-rate mortgages averaged 5.13%, 0.23 points above variable. A fixed rate is not affected by later policy moves, but the October average was higher.

Refinancing can trigger an early repayment fee. Korea's Financial Consumer Protection Act generally allows the fee only on loans repaid within three years. Whether a bank charges it when a borrower switches to a fixed rate at the same bank is set by the contract and the bank. For loans taken out from Jan. 13, 2025, fees must reflect actual costs; when the rule took effect, the Financial Services Commission said the average bank fee on variable-rate mortgages would fall from 1.25% to 0.55%. Older loans keep the fee in their original contract.

This is general information, not financial advice. Loan terms and fees vary by bank and product.

What to watch

The Korea Federation of Banks publishes November COFIX on Dec. 15. The Bank of Korea's November lending-rate figures come out in late December. Several Korean outlets reported that board members' own projections for the policy rate six months out have a median of 3.50% and a high of 3.75%. These are individual views, not decisions, and the statement does not include them.

item.title: Korea faces up to 15% in proposed Section 301 tariffs. What that adds to today's 12.5%
item.description:
The decision

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer determined on Nov. 25 that South Korea's industrial plans, preferential lending through state-owned banks and failure to address imports and investment from non-market economies are "unreasonable" and burden US commerce. That makes them actionable under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

Korea was one of 14 economies named the same day. China, the European Union, Japan, Taiwan, Vietnam and India were among the others. USTR made no determination on Mexico or Norway, the remaining two of the 16 it began investigating on March 11.

For Korea, USTR proposes tariffs on all goods of up to 15%, "net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs," with exemptions. If ongoing consultations and Korea's commitments under the Korea Strategic Trade and Investment Deal, the package set out in a joint fact sheet after Presidents Trump and Lee Jae Myung met on Nov. 13, 2025, prove unsatisfactory, it proposes up to 25% instead. Nothing changes at the border yet. These are proposals, and both figures are ceilings. USTR has not said which rate it will choose or when any tariff would start.

How it sits on today's 12.5%

Many Korean goods already carry a Section 301 duty. Since July 24, a separate action, taken after USTR found dozens of economies failed to block imports made with forced labor, has topped Korean goods up to a combined 12.5% when their regular duty rate is lower, and left them alone when it is 12.5% or higher.

The new notice uses the same wording: the 15% is "net of" the regular rate and existing Section 301 duties. We read that as a cap on the combined rate, as in July; USTR gives no worked example. On that reading, a product that pays 12.5% today gets at most 2.5 more points. For one that already pays 15% or more, it adds nothing.

Cosmetics under HTS 3304.99.50 have no regular duty. On a $10,000 shipment, the duty goes from $1,250 today to $1,500 at the 15% ceiling, $250 more. At 25% it would be $2,500.

Instant noodles under 1902.30.00 have a 6.4% regular rate and pay 12.5% in total today. They rise to 15% as well, through 6.1 points of forced-labor duty and 2.5 of the new one.

Cotton sweaters under 6110.20.20 carry 16.5%, so the 15% ceiling changes nothing. The 25% alternative would add 8.5 points, or $850 on $10,000. All four examples are before any claim under the US-Korea free trade agreement (KORUS). The notice does not say how such claims would work with the new tariff.

What stays out, and what does not

The exemptions start with goods already hit by Section 232 tariffs: articles of steel, aluminum and copper; passenger vehicles and light trucks and their parts; medium- and heavy-duty vehicles and their parts; wood products; patented pharmaceuticals; and semiconductors. Cars and the semiconductor articles covered by Section 232 would stay outside this action under the proposal. Their tariffs are set elsewhere.

Books and other informational materials, donations and accompanied baggage are also out, along with a long annex of raw materials and other goods, plus certain agglomerated iron ores.

Batteries are not on the general list. Lithium-ion batteries, HTS 8507.60.00 with a 3.4% regular rate, appear in the annex only for civil aircraft use. Batteries for grid storage and other non-aircraft uses appear to fall inside the proposal, at up to 15%, or 25% under the alternative, before any KORUS claim. Batteries entering as vehicle parts may instead fall under the Section 232 exemption. The annex sends scope questions to US Customs and Border Protection.

USTR's case against Korea

The notice lays out the numbers behind the finding. Manufacturing is 28.3% of Korea's GDP, against 9.9% in the US. Goods exports are 35.9% of GDP, against 7.1%. Korea's goods surplus with the US rose from $28.5 billion in 2021 to $55.2 billion in 2025, a nearly 94% increase.

The notice singles out chips. Two Korean companies hold more than 70% of the global DRAM market and 51% of NAND flash, the notice says, and the K-Semiconductor Belt Strategy aims to double chip exports from $100 billion in 2020 to $200 billion by 2030, backed by at least $530 billion over two decades. USTR names automotive, semiconductors and petrochemicals as sectors where the harm is especially clear. Cars and the semiconductor articles covered by Section 232 are on the proposed exempt list, though.

Seoul's written reply, summarized in the notice, says Korea runs a market economy. It argues that the surplus reflects closer supply chains in chips, cars and batteries, that Korean investment adds US production, and that it is already restructuring its petrochemical, steel and shipbuilding industries. USTR held consultations with Korea on May 27 and says they did not resolve its concerns. That reply predates the proposal; Seoul's response to the Nov. 25 notice was not available when this was written.

Next steps, and how others compare

Written comments and requests to appear are due Jan. 5, 2027, through comments.ustr.gov. The comment docket is USTR-2026-0734 and the docket for requests to appear at the hearings is USTR-2026-0741. Hearings begin Jan. 25 at the US International Trade Commission in Washington. USTR asks for views on which products to include or drop and on the rate itself.

Japan, Taiwan and Switzerland face the same "up to 15%, net of MFN" formula as Korea, and the EU a flat 15% on the same basis. Vietnam's proposal is up to 35%, net only of existing Section 301 tariffs, so the 35% would include Vietnam's existing 12.5% Section 301 duty but sit on top of the regular rate. At the full rate, Vietnamese instant noodles would pay 41.4% against Korea's 15%. USTR says Vietnam's rate could be adjusted toward 20% if it signs a reciprocal trade agreement. Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Cambodia and Bangladesh face up to 18%.

Neither cosmetics nor instant noodles are on the exempt list. In January through October 2026, Korea shipped $2.049 billion of cosmetics to the US, 37.6% more than a year earlier, and $325 million worth of the noodles, up 30.9%, according to the Korea Customs Service. Those figures cover the wider HS 3304 and 1902.30 groups, not just the tariff lines above. Export data cannot show whether tariffs changed demand. For those lines the 15% version adds 2.5 points at most; the open question is whether USTR applies the 25% alternative, which it ties to consultations and Korea's commitments.

item.title: South Korea tribunal rules state bank's meal allowance, paid inside base pay, was tax-free
item.description:
The ruling

South Korea's Tax Tribunal, which hears taxpayer appeals against the National Tax Service, ruled on July 1, 2026 that the employees of a state-owned policy bank had been overtaxed because their lunch money was paid inside their base salary. The published decision (case 2025-Seo-2281) covers income tax withheld for 2019 and 2020. The bank's name is redacted, but the decision says it was founded in 1961 to provide credit to small businesses and listed in December 2003.

Following a government push to simplify public-sector pay, the bank cut its daily lunch allowance in 2000 and moved the difference into base pay. In 2003, after a deal with the union, it ended the separate lunch payment and folded a fixed monthly amount into base pay. The pay rules never said that base pay included meal money, and throughout that time the bank withheld income tax on the amount.

On Dec. 28, 2023 its pay committee approved wording for the 2024 pay rules stating that monthly base pay includes a lunch allowance. The bank then filed to recover past tax: on March 11, 2024 for 2019 and on Jan. 2, 2025 for 2020. The local tax office refused both times.

What the law says

Article 12 of the Income Tax Act lists many tax-exempt items, including two that matter here: meals an employer provides, such as in a company cafeteria, and a meal allowance of up to 200,000 won ($149) a month for workers who are not given meals. The cap took effect on Jan. 1, 2023. Before that, an enforcement decree set it at 100,000 won ($74) a month.

The tax office pointed out that neither the employment contracts nor the pay slips showed a meal line, and the pay rules gave no basis for one. Before the tribunal, the tax office cited written interpretations by the National Tax Service from 2004 and 2006 saying that meal money rolled into annual salary without its own rule or line item is taxable.

The tribunal sided with the bank. It pointed to how state banks folded allowances into base pay under the government's early-2000s pay reform, a 2002 union activity report, the Dec. 28, 2023 pay committee minutes recording that both sides knew meal money was in base pay, the 2024 pay-rule amendment, and the fact that three other state-owned policy banks apply the exemption. The decision also records, from the bank's own submissions, that the head-office cafeteria is run by a separate committee and charges staff the same price as outsiders.

Who else this could apply to

The decision rests on this bank's documents and does not automatically extend to other employers. What follows is our reading of the issues the case turned on. The tax office argued that both the fact that pay included meal money and the amount had to be pinned down in documents.

The first question is whether the employer provides meals. The Income Tax Act covers the cash allowance only for workers who are not given meals, so a free canteen can rule out the exemption. The second is proof that a meal allowance is being paid: a salary contract, pay rules, a union agreement or a company notice stating that pay includes meal money. The third is the annual withholding statement. If the full cap for that year is already shown as tax-exempt, there is nothing to recover; if less was exempted, the difference may be claimable.

This bank submitted union records, internal approvals and pay committee minutes and was still turned down by the tax office, which also argued that staff had chosen a higher base salary, feeding into bonuses and severance, over a tax exemption. Without paperwork, the outcome at the tribunal could differ.

What it is worth in a year

If 200,000 won a month of a salary is meal money and is treated as exempt, taxable pay falls by 2.4 million won ($1,787) a year. How much tax that saves depends on income and deductions. We ran 2026 rates for a single worker who takes only the basic personal deduction and the standard tax credit.

On a 50 million won salary ($37,230), tax including the 10% local surcharge falls from 3,726,250 won to 3,350,050 won, a saving of 376,200 won ($280). On 80 million won it is 601,920 won ($448), and on 35 million won it is 354,200 won ($264). For 2021 and 2022 the cap was 100,000 won a month, so the exempt amount was 1.2 million won a year, and those years have to be worked out with that year's rates and deductions.

Actual refunds will vary. Pension contributions, dependants and card or medical deductions change taxable income and the bracket. Lower total pay can also change other deductions that depend on income. The ruling did not deal with pension or health insurance contributions; those follow separate laws, and recovering them is a separate matter from the income tax claim.

How far back, and who files

Paragraph 5 of Article 45-2 of the Framework Act on National Taxes lets an employee taxed through year-end settlement file a refund claim personally, not just the employer. The claim goes to the head of the competent tax office. The window is five years after the payment deadline for year-end tax, which is March 10 of the following year; a deadline falling on a weekend or holiday moves to the next working day. This applies to workers whose only income is wages settled at year-end. Small employers approved to pay withholding tax twice a year, and workers who filed a separate income tax return, may face different dates.

As of Nov. 26, 2026, that leaves the 2021 through 2025 tax years open. The 2021 year closes on March 10, 2027. The 2020 year closed on March 10, 2026. The bank's March 11, 2024 claim for 2019 fell inside its window.

An employer can claim for all staff at once, or employees can claim individually. In this case the disputes turned on the withholding statement and pay slips, and on documents showing that pay included meal money and that no meals were provided: salary contracts, pay rules, union agreements and company notices. A refusal can be challenged within 90 days of notice, through an objection or a request for review within the tax service, or by appeal to the Tax Tribunal. This is general information, not tax or legal advice.

The employer's side

Employers do the withholding. If one treats pay as tax-exempt and the tax office later disagrees, the employer has to pay the tax it did not withhold and can face a late-payment penalty under Article 47-5 of the Framework Act. The bank's own pay committee minutes say it added the wording in order to apply the exemption.

On the tribunal's reading, the bank's employees had paid tax on money that was exempt, and amounts older than five years are hard to recover through a refund claim. The tribunal asked whether meal money was included in base pay. The tax office argued there was no separate line and that the lunch allowance had been abolished and turned into salary.

What comes next

Under Article 80 of the Framework Act, the tax office must act in line with the decision. The refund amount is redacted. The ruling does not apply automatically to other workers' claims, and as of Nov. 26 we found no announcement that the 2004 and 2006 interpretations the tax office relied on have changed. Similar claims are decided case by case, starting at the tax office.

item.title: Cards overtake cash in euro area shops for the first time, ECB survey finds
item.description:
A first at the till

The European Central Bank first studied how euro area households use cash in 2016. Its broader survey of payment attitudes, known as SPACE, followed in 2019, 2022 and 2024. The fourth edition, published on Nov. 25, polled 51,551 people across the euro area in two waves, from September to November 2025 and from March to May 2026.

At physical points of sale such as shops, restaurants and vending machines, cards accounted for 45% of transactions and cash for 44%. It is the first time cards have come out ahead by number since comparable data began. By value, cards already made up 51%. Mobile payments, made with a phone or watch, rose to 9% from 6% in 2024.

Used less, still wanted

Across all day-to-day payments, including online purchases and money sent between people, the shift is sharper. Cash made up 68% of transactions in 2019 and 35% in 2026, roughly half its former share. Cards rose from 25% to 43% over the same period. By value, cash fell from 48% to 25%.

Cards are being used for ever-smaller sums. The average card payment shrank from €59 in 2019 to €35 in 2026. Even so, cash remains the most used method for payments under €20, and it covered 44% of payments between people.

Habits have moved faster than preferences. In shops, 54% of consumers prefer cards or other cashless methods, 22% prefer cash and 23% have no clear preference, figures almost unchanged since 2022. Some 82% said being able to pay digitally matters to them, and 62% said the same of cash. Only 3% never use cash at all.

One currency, many wallets

Countries differ widely, though the ECB notes that Germany's figures, collected by the Bundesbank, are not fully comparable with the rest. Austria has the strongest preference for cash in shops, at 39%, and Finland the weakest, at 10%. For payments between people, Germans used cash 62% of the time, compared with 26% in Finland.

Refusals run both ways. In every euro area country, at least 12% of consumers had a card or mobile payment turned down at least once in the month before the survey; 6% had cash refused. The share who find cash easy to get fell to 85% from 87% in 2024, and 19% of those who tried an ATM in the past year ran into difficulties.

A law to keep cash at the counter

The EU wants to curb such refusals by law. In 2023 the European Commission proposed a regulation clarifying the legal tender status of euro banknotes and coins. The Council of the EU, where member state governments sit, agreed its position on Dec. 19, 2025.

Under the Council's text, retailers and service providers could not refuse cash, with exceptions for distance sales, including online, and for unattended points of sale. Businesses could still say they prefer cards or digital payments. Member states would have to track whether cash is accepted and easy to obtain, and act where it is not. The text is a negotiating mandate, so it must still be agreed with the European Parliament.

The same day, the Council also agreed a position on a separate regulation for a digital euro. Piero Cipollone, a member of its Executive Board, said the bank would safeguard cash while preparing for a possible digital euro. Whether and when to issue one is for the ECB to decide once the legislation is in place.

Korea guards the other door

South Korea, where most payments are already made by card, legislated the reverse. Article 19 of the Specialized Credit Financial Business Act bars merchants from refusing a credit card payment, or treating card users less favorably, because they pay by card. Breaking the rule can bring up to a year in prison or a fine of up to 10 million won (about $7,000). Korean banknotes are legal tender for all transactions under the Bank of Korea Act, but none of the act's penalty clauses (Articles 104 to 105-2) covers a shop that turns cash away.

Korea's cash share is lower. In a 2024 Bank of Korea survey of 3,551 adults, credit cards made up 46.2% of payments by number, debit cards 16.4% and cash 15.9%, down from 41.3% in 2013 and 26.4% in 2019. The two surveys use different methods, so the figures are not directly comparable. Still, 88.0% of Korean adults said they had used cash in a face-to-face purchase in the previous month.

Europe's shift toward cards resembles Korea's. The difference is that the EU wants to add a legal duty to accept cash. If the Council and Parliament agree, the rule would apply across the euro area, subject to the exceptions above.

item.title: The 2027 conforming loan limit rises to $855,400, but the Denver and Seattle metro areas stay put
item.description:
What changed on Nov. 24

Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the two government-sponsored mortgage companies, will be able to buy one-unit home loans of up to $855,400 in most of the United States in 2027. The Federal Housing Finance Agency announced the figure on Nov. 24, and it takes effect on Jan. 1. That is $22,650 more than this year's $832,750. Under the Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008, the baseline moves with FHFA's house price index, which the agency reports rose 2.72% between the third quarters of 2025 and 2026. In 3,071 of the country's 3,235 counties and county equivalents, the baseline is the limit.

The number decides which mortgages count as conforming. A loan above the limit for its county is generally considered a jumbo loan, which the two companies cannot buy. In high-cost areas the limit can reach $1,283,100, which is 150% of the baseline. Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the US Virgin Islands start from $1,283,100 and top out at $1,924,650.

This is general information, not tax, legal or financial advice. Whether a particular loan qualifies is up to the lender.

The 24 counties that did not move

FHFA said limits rise in all but 24 counties or county equivalents. Its release does not name them, so we compared the agency's 2026 and 2027 county files, 3,235 rows each. Thirteen of the 24 are in Colorado, including all 10 counties of the Denver metro area, which stay at $862,500. King, Pierce and Snohomish counties, the Seattle metro area, stay at $1,063,750.

The other 11: Garfield and Pitkin in Colorado at $1,209,750 and San Miguel at $994,750; Napa at $1,017,750 and Sonoma at $897,000 in California; Maui and Kalawao in Hawaii at $1,299,500; Calvert County, Md., Pike County, Pa., and Madison County, Va., all at $1,209,750; and Wayne County, Utah, at $997,050.

A flat limit is not a lower limit. FHFA sets a high-cost limit at 115% of the area's median home value, using values estimated by the Federal Housing Administration, and it has a practice of never letting a limit fall. Its methodology note says each 2027 limit is the higher of the new formula result and past limits. In these 24 places the formula did not beat this year's number, so the old one carries over. The release and the note do not say what drove the result in each county. Nearby Boulder and Weld counties in Colorado and Kitsap County in Washington are not among the 24; their limits rise.

What a flat limit means for a buyer

These areas now have less room above the national baseline. In the Seattle metro area the local limit was $231,000 above the baseline in 2026 and will be $208,350 above it in 2027. Around Denver the gap falls from $29,750 to $7,100, which is 0.83% of the new baseline.

To see what the limit means for a purchase, divide it by one minus the down payment share. That gives the highest price a conforming loan can cover. With 20% down it is $1,069,250 at the baseline, $1,078,125 in the Denver metro area and about $1,329,700 in the Seattle metro area. With 10% down the baseline figure is about $950,400. These figures leave out closing costs, mortgage insurance and each lender's own rules.

Take a $1,080,000 house in Denver bought with 20% down. The loan would be $864,000, which is $1,500 over the county limit in both 2026 and 2027. A down payment of $217,500, about 20.1%, brings the loan to exactly $862,500. In King County, 20% down on a $1,350,000 home means a $1,080,000 loan, $16,250 over the limit, and putting $286,250 down, about 21.2%, brings it to $1,063,750.

Where the limit jumped

Six counties that were at the baseline in 2026 move above it for 2027: all five counties of Rhode Island and Bristol County, Mass., which go from $832,750 to $897,000, up $64,250. Four others reach the new $1,283,100 ceiling after sitting below it in 2026: Lake and Summit counties in Colorado, up $190,600 from $1,092,500, and Summit and Wasatch counties in Utah, up $133,100 from $1,150,000. Routt and Moffat, also in Colorado, gain $179,400 and reach $1,268,450, just under the ceiling.

In the contiguous states and D.C., 42 counties sit at the $1,283,100 ceiling in 2027, including Los Angeles, San Francisco and the District of Columbia, compared with 38 at this year's $1,249,125 ceiling. For two-, three- and four-unit homes, the 2027 baselines are $1,095,250, $1,323,900 and $1,645,350.

What to check, and what could still change

The limit that applies is the one for the county where the property sits, not where the buyer lives. FHFA's county list, sorted by state, is the reference. Federal Housing Administration loans follow a separate set of limits that FHA publishes itself.

One step remains. Once FHA announces its 2027 limits, it allows 30 days for appeals with data showing a higher median home value. If FHA revises a median after an appeal and that changes a conforming limit, FHFA says it may adjust that county's limit and announce it. Whether any county's number moves will be known only after FHA publishes its limits and the appeal window closes.

item.title: Ofgem raises Britain's energy price cap 26% for January 2027, and big gas users feel it most
item.description:
What January's bill looks like

Wholesale gas prices have roughly tripled since the conflict in the Middle East began, and that cost is now landing on British households. Ofgem, the energy regulator for England, Scotland and Wales, said on Nov. 25 that the cap on household energy prices will rise 26% from Jan. 1 to March 31, 2027. For a typical home that uses both electricity and gas and pays by Direct Debit, an automatic bank payment, the annualized bill goes from £1,723 to £2,166, or from about $2,247 to $2,825. That is £443, roughly $578, more over a year if the new level held, or about £111 ($144) a quarter. Winter use is higher, so actual January-to-March bills will run above that average.

The cap covers about 20 million households on standard variable tariffs, the default plan for anyone who has not chosen a fixed deal. Roughly 10 million households on fixed deals are not affected while their contracts last. Ofgem says that, adjusted for inflation, the new cap is 31.8% higher than in January to March 2026.

Gas rates up 38%, power rates up 24%

Ofgem points to war-driven gas prices, which it says kept climbing in recent months. At average Direct Debit rates, gas rises from 7.97p to 10.96p per kilowatt-hour, about 10 to 14 U.S. cents and up 37.5%. Electricity climbs from 26.32p to 32.69p, about 34 to 43 cents and up 24.2%. The standing charge, a flat daily fee for being connected, barely changes: 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas.

Gas still feeds a large part of Britain's power generation, so electricity prices follow gas, though less as renewables grow. Counting standing charges, Ofgem puts the rise in a typical gas bill at 33% and in an electricity bill at 19%. The government has removed the 5% value-added tax, Britain's version of a sales tax, from electricity bills from October 2026 through June 2027, but gas still carries it, so Ofgem says comparisons with periods before October 2026 are not like for like.

A cap that is not a ceiling

Despite the name, there is no maximum bill. The cap limits what suppliers may charge per kilowatt-hour and per day, so a household that uses more pays more. The £2,166 figure rests on Ofgem's typical consumption, which the regulator cut in July by about 7% for electricity and 17% for gas. On the old benchmark, the typical bill would be going from £1,935 to £2,451.

Applying the new rates to three sample homes shows who is most exposed. A home using 2,500 kWh of electricity and 9,500 kWh of gas a year goes from £1,724 to £2,167, up 26% and within a pound of Ofgem's figure. A smaller home using 1,800 kWh and 7,500 kWh goes from £1,380 to £1,719, up 25%. A large house using 4,100 kWh and 17,000 kWh goes from £2,742 to £3,512, up 28%. Because the daily fee stays flat while unit rates rise, the more energy a home uses, the larger the share of its bill exposed to the increase. The fee is 9% of the large home's January-to-March bill but 18% of the small home's.

How people pay matters too. Ofgem says switching from paying on receipt of the bill to Direct Debit saves the average customer about £160 a year. The government has announced £100 toward the bills of around 20 million households from January.

Britain passes costs on; Korea's pass-through hit its cap

Britain's regulator resets the cap every three months to reflect wholesale costs. Since the energy crisis, Ofgem says, it has tightened suppliers' financial-resilience rules so they can absorb price swings.

South Korea's power rates include a fuel-cost pass-through, and it has a ceiling. For October to December, state-controlled Korea Electric Power Corp. (KEPCO) kept its quarterly fuel-cost adjustment at 5 won, about 0.4 U.S. cent, per kilowatt-hour, freezing household rates. That adjustment is the part meant to track fuel costs, and it is already at its 5-won cap. Korea's generation mix differs from Britain's, so gas prices may not reach its costs the same way, but fuel costs that cannot be passed on can remain a burden on KEPCO's finances. When, or whether, they reach Korean bills or public budgets has not been decided.

When the next cap comes

The new rates apply to energy used from Jan. 1. Ofgem will publish the April-to-June cap by Feb. 23, 2027. The government has also asked Ofgem to remove standing charges from gas bills in 2027 or as soon as possible afterward, and the regulator is working on options.

item.title: South Korea's draft crypto law would make exchanges pay for hacks even without fault
item.description:
What the draft would change

When a Korean crypto exchange is hacked, who covers the losses? A draft law discussed on Nov. 24 by the Virtual Asset Committee, an advisory panel to the Financial Services Commission (FSC), South Korea's financial regulator, gives a direct answer: as a rule, the firm would pay, even if it was not at fault, when users lose assets to hacking or a system failure.

The bill, the Act on the Innovation of the Digital Asset Industry and User Protection, is meant as the second phase of South Korea's crypto rules, after a 2024 law that covered user protection and market abuse. That law speaks of "virtual assets"; the new one uses "digital assets". The FSC cited two recent cases: unauthorized outflows from one exchange's wallet in November 2025, and a hack at another exchange in October 2026 that leaked personal data and some assets.

It is a government proposal for new legislation. Lawmakers would have to pass it, and the FSC gave no date for submission or for the rules to take effect.

Today's rule: have money set aside

Article 8 of the current Virtual Asset User Protection Act, in force since July 2024, tells exchanges to buy insurance, join a mutual-aid scheme or build reserves so they can meet their liability for hacks and outages. It covers how a payout is funded. It does not say when a payout for a hack is owed. General civil law may apply, and much depends on the exchange's terms and the facts of the case.

The 2024 law also requires exchanges to park at least 100% of customers' won deposits with a bank or other custodian, and to keep customers' coins offline at a ratio the FSC sets, which under a government decree cannot fall below 70%.

Banks pay by default; the draft would too, with exceptions

Paying without asking whether the customer was careless is already the rule for Korean banks and electronic payment firms. Article 9 of the Electronic Financial Transactions Act makes them pay when a customer loses money through forged or altered credentials, an error in sending or processing a transaction, or credentials stolen by breaking into a network.

There are two carve-outs. If the customer acted intentionally or with gross negligence and agreed in advance to bear such a loss, the bank can shift some or all of it to the customer; what counts as gross negligence is limited to what the terms of service list, within bounds set by decree. Separately, a bank can shift a loss suffered by a corporate customer, other than a small business, if it followed proper security procedures and took reasonable care.

The draft has carve-outs too. An attachment to the FSC's announcement says that, as a rule, the firm pays, but users also bear responsibility where they acted intentionally or with gross negligence, or where the terms of service provide for it. It reads close to the bank rule, but the one-line summary does not show whether, as for banks, gross negligence and a prior agreement are both required or each applies on its own. Neither the announcement nor the attachment says how far terms of service could go, whether account takeovers or phishing count as hacking, or whether payouts would be capped. Those answers will sit in the bill text, which has not been published.

What exchanges stand to lose

On top of compensation, the FSC could impose punitive fines of up to 10% of revenue on a digital asset firm whose failure to meet bank-level security duties leads to an incident. Assuming revenue of 1 trillion won ($744 million), the cap would be 100 billion won, about $74 million. Neither the announcement nor the attachment defines which revenue, or over what period, counts. Hacks and outages would have to be disclosed immediately, and the draft adds a basis for criminal punishment of anyone who steals assets by hacking trading facilities.

The attachment says custodians that offer staking would face an extra insurance requirement for hacks and similar incidents. It gives no other funding rules. The FSC says it heard industry and expert views on Nov. 23, but it gives only a general summary and no industry reaction to the liability or ownership rules.

A proposed 20% cap on exchange owners

The FSC could designate as an exchange operator only a firm that holds all three licenses: dealing (trading for its own account), brokerage and custody. To keep exchanges neutral, the bill borrows the ownership rule for Korea's alternative stock trading venues: no shareholder could own more than 20%, though the FSC plans to allow financial firms and similar holders up to 34% with its approval. Any shares above the cap could not be voted.

The cap would not bite right away. Existing exchanges would get a three-year grace period after designation, and those that are small or mid-sized by market share could get three more, for up to six years in all. Newly designated exchanges would be treated the same way. Neither the announcement nor the attachment says whether stakes held by related parties would be added together.

Dealing, brokerage and custody licenses would come with capital floors to be set by decree: 2 billion won ($1.5 million) for firms handling all digital assets and 1 billion won ($744,000) for stablecoin-only firms. Asset managers, which would only register because they do not hold client assets, would need 500 million won ($372,000).

Who could issue a stablecoin in Korea

The bill calls stablecoins "digital payment tokens": assets pegged to a single currency and used mainly for payments. Issuers in Korea would need an FSC license and at least 5 billion won ($3.7 million) in equity. The shareholder rules would be set by decree, and the FSC plans to start with consortiums in which banks hold a majority, though a fintech or tech company could be the largest single shareholder. Foreign issuers supervised at home could also operate through a registered local branch.

Issuers would have to keep reserves of at least 100% of tokens outstanding with a bank or similar custodian, ring-fenced from creditors. If the issuer lost its license, went bankrupt or could not redeem normally after a hack, the custodian would pay holders first. Holders could not be paid interest.

The FSC could label a token significant, looking at user numbers and issuance of 1 trillion won or more, among other things, where it could affect financial stability or monetary policy. Significant issuers would face extra capital, tighter reserve liquidity management and risk controls, and the Bank of Korea could demand data and joint inspections. The FSC says the EU uses a threshold of 5 billion euros and the U.S. $10 billion, roughly 7.3 trillion won and 13.4 trillion won at Nov. 24 exchange rates. By those figures, Korea's line sits at about a seventh of the EU's and a thirteenth of the U.S. level. The announcement treats 1 trillion won as a threshold while the attachment lists it as one factor, so whether it stands alone will depend on the bill text. The three regimes are not built the same way, and in Korea crossing the line would not trigger the label automatically.

Token sales and market abuse

Initial coin offerings, which South Korea has barred at home, would be allowed with disclosure. Issuers would file a white paper, similar to a securities registration statement, and wait out a review period before selling. Exchanges would have to file and publish a report before listing a token. The FSC pointed to a September 2026 case in which a currency-pegged stablecoin jumped to 4.2 times its reference price right after listing because supply was short, settling only eight hours later.

Market-abuse rules would widen to cover tokens still under listing review and swaps between coins, so that exchanges that do not trade against the won are also covered. With substantial suspicion, the FSC could freeze accounts, and whistleblowers could be paid rewards.

Until then

The FSC said only that it would support quick passage in the National Assembly. Until a law passes, today's rules stay in place: insurance or reserves, bank custody for won deposits, offline storage for most coins, and, for claims, general civil law and the exchange's terms.

This is general information about how the rules work, not legal or investment advice.

item.title: South Korea's draft rule would exempt AI data centers up to 50 MW from grid review outside the Seoul area
item.description:
The 40 MW question

Suppose a company wants to build a 40-megawatt AI data center in South Korea outside the Seoul metropolitan area, which covers Seoul, Incheon and Gyeonggi Province. If the site is in a designated area, today's rules require a grid impact assessment before it applies for permits: a review of whether the local power network can handle a big new load. Under draft decrees published on Nov. 20 by the Ministry of Science and ICT, it would skip that step if the rule is finalized as written.

The decrees flesh out the Special Act on the Promotion of the AI Data Center Industry, which was promulgated on June 9, 2026 and takes effect on March 10, 2027. Comments are open until Dec. 30, and a public hearing is set for Dec. 9 in Seoul.

From 10 MW to 50 MW

The current threshold sits in Article 25 of the enforcement decree of the Distributed Energy Act. In areas designated by the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment, any business planning to draw 10 MW or more must be assessed. The report is due three months before the business applies for permits, and the government has three months after receiving it to notify the outcome.

Article 17 of the draft would exempt new, expanded or converted AI data centers outside the Seoul metropolitan area with contracted power of 50 MW or less. Contracted power is the maximum load a customer agrees with the utility, not actual use. That moves the line five times higher. A 50 MW site running flat out for all 8,760 hours of a year would use 438 gigawatt-hours; a 10 MW site would use 87.6 GWh. Actual use depends on how busy the servers are.

There is a precedent. Article 26 of the same decree already allows exemptions for projects in national strategic high-tech industries. AI data centers are not named there; the new act sets a threshold of its own.

What counts as an AI data center

To get the exemption, a site must first qualify. Article 3 of the draft measures AI equipment power, the electricity designed to feed racks of GPUs, NPUs and other AI accelerators. A site qualifies with at least 250 kilowatts of AI equipment power that makes up 50% or more of its total IT power, or with at least 5 MW of AI equipment power. The ratio and size figures are set by ministry notice.

Take a site with 2 MW of IT power. If 1.2 MW goes to AI racks, the share is 60% and it qualifies; with 0.9 MW, the share is 45% and it misses the ratio test. There is an efficiency test too: total facility power divided by IT power must be 1.5 or lower at the design stage, which the ministry says works out to roughly 1.3 to 1.4 in operation. Sites also need cooling, backup power, fire safety and security systems. Colocation sites that rent out space and power for other companies' AI racks are covered.

Who saves time, who carries the cost

Developers gain time and space. Skipping the review can shorten the permit schedule, and under a bundled-permit track, if a related agency does not reply within 10 days, the process moves ahead on the documents already filed. Required on-site parking can be cut by 20%, and local ordinances can ease it further, to as little as half the standard. Server rooms can also be left out of the floor area used to set Korea's mandatory public-art spending for new buildings: all of it outside the Seoul area, half inside it.

What remains is the grid. Skipping the review does not make a big new load any smaller. The government said it weighed industry demands against the effect of large AI data centers on regional networks and settled on 50 MW. The ministries also noted that raising the line to 100 MW would still leave most gigawatt-scale projects outside it, so they agreed on two parallel measures instead.

The draft also targets developers that file plans and never build. A company filing a construction notice must set a construction start date within one year of filing, a step meant to stop firms from locking in the exemption without breaking ground. In short, developers would save paperwork and waiting time; the job of expanding regional grids stays.

Two related measures

Two separate measures, to be set by the climate ministry through a notice and a work manual rather than the decree, apply regardless of size. An 'AIDC fast track' puts reviews for mega projects and bundled-permit data centers at the front of the queue. Inside AI data center zones, which local governments apply for, data centers would skip the non-technical part of the review and face only the technical part, though the scoring for power demand may be adjusted.

In those zones, central and local governments could build or fund roads, heat supply and energy storage, waste-heat reuse, high-speed networks and facilities for nearby residents, on top of power and water. The ministry has 90 days to review a zone application before the National AI Strategy Committee decides. Numbers can still change after comments close on Dec. 30, so developers should check the contracted-power threshold again in the final decree.

item.title: Fed's Williams points to AI chip demand in U.S. inflation as Korean chips fetch 2.7 times more per kilogram
item.description:
Three causes, one of them chips

Inflation is "simply too high," John Williams, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, said on Nov. 23 at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in the Bronx. The Fed's preferred gauge, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, is running at about 3.5%, well above the 2% target. As head of the New York Fed, Williams holds a permanent vote on the Federal Open Market Committee, which sets rates.

He traced the problem to three sources. Tariffs come first, though he said their effect on inflation has largely faded. Next are supply-chain disruptions and high energy and commodity prices tied to the conflicts in the Middle East. The third is the AI boom: prices of goods essential to the buildout, especially semiconductors, have risen sharply, and so far demand is clearly outpacing supply.

A hike in September, a pause in October

The Fed raised its target range by a quarter point to 3.75%-4% on Sept. 17, its first increase since July 2023. On Oct. 28 it held, in a 10-2 vote; both dissenters wanted another quarter-point hike.

Minutes of that meeting, released Nov. 18, show most participants backed the pause. Many of them wanted to see how durable AI investment demand would be, how financing conditions would evolve and how the September hike would work through the economy. A couple of participants said a gradual approach to tightening would give businesses and households time to adjust. Williams said on Monday that getting inflation back to 2% will take action over time, and that there is still work to do.

A gauge from Korea

Williams did not say how much chip prices have risen. South Korea, home to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, two of the world's biggest memory makers, offers a rough gauge, though not one he cited. According to Korea Customs Service data, the country's chip exports (integrated circuits, HS code 8542) rose 203.7% to $40.02 billion in October 2026 from $13.18 billion a year earlier. Their weight rose only 10.5%, from 1,592 metric tons to 1,759 metric tons.

Divide value by weight and a kilogram of Korean chips was worth $22,756 in October, 2.75 times the $8,276 of a year earlier. The figure peaked at $24,114 in September and slipped 5.6% in October.
