It blends price increases with a shift toward pricier products, so it is not a price index. Value tripled while weight rose 10.5%, but these data cannot separate higher prices from a richer product mix. The biggest buyers are China, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Vietnam. In the 12 months to October 2026, Korea shipped $127.2 billion of chips to China, $53.7 billion to Taiwan, $50.2 billion to Hong Kong and $46.9 billion to Vietnam, against $3.27 billion directly to the United States.

So these figures cannot say how much of Korea's export value ends up in U.S. consumer prices. What they show is a steep rise in the value of Korean chip exports, consistent with the strong AI demand Williams described.

What would change the Fed's math

Williams called the AI risks to inflation two-sided. If the buildout slows, much of the AI-driven inflation could reverse; if investment speeds up and supply cannot keep pace, prices could climb further. Elsewhere he saw relief: housing costs have slowed, and he found no sign that wages are pushing inflation up.

He expects inflation of about 3.5% this year, just above 2% next year and 2% in 2028. That path assumes energy prices normalize and supply and demand for AI-related goods come back into balance. Korea's chip value per kilogram fell 5.6% in October from September. It also dipped once in January before climbing again, so one month is too early to read as the start of that rebalancing.

Dates to watch

The Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes October PCE inflation at 8:30 a.m. Eastern on Nov. 25, alongside its second estimate of third-quarter GDP. The FOMC meets Dec. 8-9. Korea's trade ministry is scheduled to release November export totals on Dec. 1, and customs data by product, with weights, follow later in the month. The December rate decision has not been made.

item.title: South Korea orders large employers to disclose workplace safety records, including contractor deaths
item.description:
Who has to file, and what

South Korea's new safety filing includes a line for contractor workers killed in accidents at the main contractor's own workplace. In other words, when a subcontractor's worker is killed in an accident at the plant or site of a big company that hires contractors, that company records it under its own name. On Nov. 23 the Ministry of Employment and Labor, together with the Korea Employers Federation, the main business lobby, briefed covered companies on a draft guide for the filings.

The rule is Article 10-2 of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, added by an amendment promulgated on Feb. 19, 2026, and in force since Aug. 1. The enforcement decree applies it to employers with 500 or more regular workers, and to builders with at least 120 billion won (about $89 million) of construction work a year. The law names public institutions and local public corporations (companies owned by city and provincial governments) separately and sets no headcount threshold for them.

The law lists six items: the safety management system, workplace accidents, last year's safety activities and this year's plan, safety spending, measures to prevent repeat accidents, and a sixth left to the decree. The decree fills it in two ways. Firms that hire contractors must report contractor workers killed in accidents at their sites. Public bodies that commission construction projects worth 5 billion won (about $3.7 million) or more must report deaths in accidents on those projects, of both the main contractor's and subcontractors' workers.

This is general information about the rules, not legal advice.

How this differs from what the government already publishes

Folding contractor accidents into the main company's record is not new in itself. Under Article 10 of the same law, the labor minister publishes accident counts and rates for workplaces such as those with two or more work-related deaths in a year. Contractor accidents are added in two ways: at such sites where the main company broke its duty to protect contractor workers and they were hurt, and at manufacturing, rail, urban rail and power sites where the main company has 500 or more regular workers and the accident death rate including contractors is higher than its own. Construction is not covered by the second route.

The government's publication stays, and company filings come on top of it. Three things are new. Companies file for themselves: a ministry ordinance says each filer must post the record, confirmed by its chief executive, on a ministry-designated website by April 30 each year. Every covered company files, not only sites with bad accident records. And spending and plans appear alongside accident figures.

For public construction, deaths on a site the public body does not run will now appear in the commissioning body's own filing, for projects of 5 billion won or more.

Is a 10 million won fine the whole story?

Failing to file carries a fine of up to 10 million won, about $7,400. The decree sets 10 million won as the standard for a first, second or third violation, and allows it to be cut by up to half in some circumstances. For a company with 500 or more workers that is small money.

The rule may carry more weight with the people who read the numbers. Once filings are posted, a contractor worker can see the deaths a main company recorded at its sites before taking a job there. For the main company, spending plans and accident figures will sit in the same place each year, so a gap between promise and outcome can show. Investors, clients commissioning work and job seekers may get material to compare companies in the same industry.

The enforcement tools are thin. The ministry can ask for corrections, additions or supporting documents if a filing looks wrong or incomplete. But under the act, its enforcement decree and the ministry ordinance, the fine applies only to failing to file; no provision sets a separate penalty for understating the numbers, unlike false data on contractors submitted for the government's own publication, which can be fined. How comparable the filings turn out to be depends on the reporting standards in the final guide.

How the US does it

The US Occupational Safety and Health Administration has collected injury and illness summaries electronically since 2016 and now offers the data for download establishment by establishment. Establishments with 250 or more employees, outside exempt industries, file a summary, as do those with 20 to 249 in listed industries. Since 2024, establishments with 100 or more employees in designated industries also submit case-level records. The 2026 filing deadline was March 2.

The two systems measure different things. The US data is a record of injuries and illnesses at each site; Korea's filing is by company and adds the management system, spending and plans. OSHA's description of its data does not include a separate count of contractor deaths under the host company's name. OSHA also notes that a recorded injury does not mean the employer was at fault or broke a rule, a caution worth keeping in mind with Korea's figures too.

Dec. 10, and then April 2027

The draft guide is open for public comment from Nov. 20 to Dec. 10 on the ministry's website (moel.go.kr), and anyone can respond. The Korea Employers Federation said it would pass on companies' views so that the standards reflect conditions on the ground.

The rules set no special date for the first year, so the first deadline is the first April 30 after Aug. 1, which is April 30, 2027. To report contractor deaths, main companies will likely need accident records from their suppliers well before then. Korean media covering the draft guide reported that the first filings would be made public from June 2027. The guide is not final, so the timing and format could change.

item.title: What is a chaebol? Samsung, Hyundai and Korea's family-run business groups explained
item.description:
The short answer

A chaebol is a group of Korean companies controlled by one person or family through shareholdings that run from company to company. Samsung, SK, Hyundai Motor and LG are the four biggest. The Samsung phone, the Hyundai SUV and the LG fridge in an American home each come from a different company, but each of those companies sits inside a group of many others.

The Korea Fair Trade Commission, the country's antitrust regulator, tracks them as large business groups. Each group has a "same person" (dongilin in Korean), the individual or company the commission treats as controlling it and as ultimately responsible for following the rules for large groups. For Samsung that is Lee Jae-yong, for SK Chey Tae-won, for Hyundai Motor Chung Eui-sun and for LG Koo Kwang-mo. The commission's list is a regulatory category, not a legal definition of chaebol. Of this year's 102 groups, 13 have no controlling person; some are run by a company or by a cooperative federation.

How many, and how big

Every spring the commission names the groups big enough to face extra rules. As of May 1, 2026, it designated 102 groups with at least 5 trillion won in assets, about $3.7 billion at 1,343.6 won to the dollar, the rate on Nov. 23. They include 3,538 companies. All of them must disclose large deals between their own companies and may not give unfair benefits to the controlling family. The 47 largest, each with at least 12 trillion won (about $8.9 billion), an amount set at 0.5% of Korea's 2,408.7 trillion won GDP, face more. Their companies may not hold shares in each other or create new circular shareholdings, guarantee each other's debts, or freely vote affiliates' shares held by their financial and insurance arms.

Samsung tops the list with 67 companies and 695.8 trillion won in assets on the commission's measure, about $518 billion. That is 18.1% more than a year earlier, a period in which the group also went from 63 companies to 67. SK follows with 422.0 trillion won, Hyundai Motor with 320.8 trillion and LG with 186.3 trillion. We added up the assets of all 102 groups: the top four hold 44.3% of them.

Control with 3.5% of the shares

How can a family run companies it barely owns? The commission's September report on the 89 groups that have a controlling person shows the numbers. Across their Korean member companies, weighted by capital, the family directly owns 3.5% of the shares on average. The group's own companies own 55.5%. Add shares held by group nonprofits and executives, and shares the companies have bought back from the market, and insiders hold 61.4%. The average hides a wide range. At Iljin Global, the controlling person himself owns 51.4% of the group's shares, the highest of any group.

Picture the average as 1,000 shares. The family holds 35. Affiliates hold 555, and other insiders about 24, a figure we got by subtraction. That leaves 386 with outside shareholders. In some groups the family owns a large stake in a company near the top, often a holding company that exists mainly to own shares in others, and that company owns the next ones down. The commission says the gap between direct family ownership and insider holdings across the group remains substantial.

Circular shareholdings, in which company A owns B, B owns C and C owns A, fell across the 102 groups from 1,435 loops in 2025 to 233 in 2026. More than the whole net drop came from one group, Sajo, which cut its loops from 1,426 to 220. Sales between a group's own companies were large. In 2025, 35.0% of the revenue of 2,871 Korean member companies, 841 trillion won or about $626 billion, came from selling to affiliates: 11.5% to affiliates in Korea and 23.5% to affiliates abroad. The commission says such deals can cut transaction costs, but can also be used to hand unfair gains to particular affiliates.

Where Americans run into them

Most Americans meet a chaebol as a shopper. Some meet one as a worker. Samsung announced an estimated $17 billion chip plant in Taylor, Texas, in November 2021, its largest US investment at the time. SK hynix, part of the SK group, agreed in April 2024 to invest an estimated $3.87 billion in a chip packaging plant in West Lafayette, Indiana, with more than 1,000 jobs.

Investors in Coupang, the e-commerce company listed in New York, meet the rules too. Coupang is among the 102 designated groups. Until this year the commission listed the company itself, not a person, as the group's same person. On April 29 it named founder Bom Kim instead, effective May 1. It found that his brother held a vice-president-level role at Coupang and had chaired hundreds of meetings on delivery policy, so Coupang no longer met the legal conditions for a company to be named. The commission said it wanted the same person to match whoever actually controls the group.

What changed in 2025 and 2026

For investors, the open question has long been whose interest a chaebol board serves. Korea's Commercial Act now answers part of it. An amendment promulgated in July 2025 says directors must act for the company and its shareholders and treat all shareholders fairly. Before, the law named only the company.

A second amendment, promulgated on Sept. 9, 2025, took effect on Sept. 10, 2026. Listed companies above an asset threshold set by decree can no longer write cumulative voting out of their articles of incorporation. Shareholders with at least 1% of the voting shares must still ask for it in writing six weeks before the meeting. When they do, a shareholder voting in an election for three directors gets three votes per share and can put them all on one candidate, which makes it easier for minority holders to seat a director. The same law raised the number of audit committee members elected separately from the other directors from one to at least two at listed companies that must have an audit committee.

The cumulative-voting rule applies from the first shareholders' meeting called to elect directors after Sept. 10, 2026. The commission's next data release, on how group boards are run, is due in December.

item.title: Kakao Pay and Toss now verify Korean ID cards. Opt-in blocks can stop loans and accounts in your name
item.description:
What the payment apps now check

Anyone who has signed up for a Korean payment app knows the routine: hold your national ID card up to the phone camera and wait. From Nov. 23, the Ministry of the Interior and Safety said, Kakao Pay and Toss would run that ID card through a government system as well, using its national ID verification service for remote customer checks. Naver Pay plans to join in December.

Banks, brokerages and insurers already used the service. Kakao Pay and Toss are licensed as electronic financial businesses, the category for payment firms that are not banks. They are the first in that group that can check not only that the name, resident registration number and issue date printed on a card are valid, but also whether the card itself is genuine, using photo data. The ministry called it a bank-level check.

Kakao Pay ran about 7.5 million remote customer checks in 2025 and Toss about 10 million. Together that is 17.5 million, or roughly 48,000 a day.

This is general information about how the system works, not legal or financial advice.

Why the photo matters

Forged ID cards are a working tool for fraud. In March 2025 the Financial Services Commission (FSC), the main financial regulator, described a case in which criminals used a malicious app to lift personal data from a victim's phone, opened a budget mobile line in the victim's name, passed identity verification with a forged ID card and quietly opened an account at an internet-only bank. That bank was not one of these apps. The criminals then stole tens of millions of won.

The ministry did not describe how the two apps checked cards before. It set out who may use the system and how in a notice issued on July 27, and the Korea Financial Telecommunications and Clearings Institute connected the two apps through the relay that banks already use. The Financial Supervisory Service said it inspected the three firms' ID-checking technology and operations beforehand.

What the check does not cover

The announcement is about the national ID card. It does not say how other documents, such as driver's licenses, are checked, and Naver Pay users are not covered until December. The ministry says it will extend the service across electronic financial businesses but has not said which ones or when.

Nor does it claim to stop a criminal who holds a real ID card or controls the victim's phone remotely. Someone with stolen personal data could still try to borrow or open an account at another lender. Separately from the ID check, the FSC has since August 2024 rolled out opt-in blocks that let people stop such new transactions themselves.

Three blocks you can set yourself

The first is a block on new loans. Launched on Aug. 23, 2024, it records a flag with the Korea Credit Information Services and new remote credit in the person's name, including personal loans, credit-card loans, new credit cards, installment finance and loans against deposits, is refused in real time. A total of 4,012 financial companies joined at launch. On May 16, 2025, the FSC said users would be able to choose whether the block also covers new credit cards.

The second, from March 12, 2025, stops anyone opening an ordinary demand-deposit account in the person's name remotely, the kind of account fraud rings use to receive stolen money. A total of 3,613 institutions take part, including banks, savings banks, cooperatives and the postal bank.

The third, from Nov. 14, 2025, covers open banking, the shared system that lets one app view and move money across accounts at different institutions. Users pick which institutions to block. All accounts there are then barred from open banking registration, and accounts already registered can no longer be viewed or drawn on through it. A total of 3,608 institutions take part.

Uptake surged in spring 2025. The loan block had 89,817 users on Sept. 26, 2024 and about 310,000 in March 2025, then 2.55 million on May 12. The FSC said that in the three weeks from April 22 to May 12, after a hacking incident at the mobile carrier SK Telecom, loan-block sign-ups rose by 2.12 million and account-block sign-ups by 1.88 million. It said this appeared to reflect identity-theft worries, especially among young and middle-aged adults. In its Nov. 14, 2025 announcement it gave figures for the end of October 2025: about 3.18 million people with the loan block and about 2.52 million with the account block.

How to sign up

People can apply at a branch of a bank, savings bank, farm, fishery or forestry cooperative, credit union, community credit cooperative (Saemaeul Geumgo) or post office where they already have an account, or in a bank's mobile app. The account and open banking blocks can also be set in AccountInfo, an app run by the Korea Financial Telecommunications and Clearings Institute. The loan block was branch-only at first; the FSC said the three internet-only banks, KakaoBank, Toss Bank and K Bank, would take applications in their apps from Sept. 30, 2024 (K Bank from Oct. 8).

Family members can act for older relatives. On May 16, 2025, the FSC said a relative with valid authorization would be able to set or lift the loan and account blocks: a spouse, the spouse's parents, parents, grandparents, children, grandchildren, and sons- or daughters-in-law.

Users can check their status later: the account block on the credit information service's website, credit4u.or.kr, and the open banking block in AccountInfo or a bank app. Institutions send a reminder by text or email twice a year for the loan and account blocks and once a year for open banking.

The catch

The block works on its owner too. Someone who needs a loan or a new account must go to a branch to lift it. The FSC says an account block, once lifted, allows a new account to be opened straight away. For the loan block, staff check that the request is not being made under pressure from a scammer. The open banking block can be lifted only after a face-to-face identity check at a branch.

The FSC said it set that rule so that fraudsters cannot remove the block. It also means that anyone with a block who later needs a loan or a new account has to make a branch visit first.

It helps to know the scope. The FSC describes the blocks as stopping new remote loans, new remote accounts, and open banking registration, withdrawals and views. It does not say whether they stop a transfer the owner makes after being tricked, or a withdrawal that does not go through open banking.

item.title: South Korea gives savers three years after maturity to turn savings insurance into an annuity
item.description:
What changes on Dec. 1

South Korean life insurers will give customers more time to turn a matured savings policy into an annuity. From Dec. 1, 2026, a policyholder who has not yet collected the maturity payout can apply to convert it into an annuity for up to three years after the policy matures, the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS), the country's financial regulator, and the Korea Life Insurance Association said on Nov. 19.

The product is savings-type life insurance: the customer pays premiums for a set term, the insurer credits interest, and the balance is paid out at maturity. Most of these policies carry a rider that lets the holder take the money as an annuity instead of a lump sum. Until now most life insurers accepted that request only on the maturity date itself. Miss the day and the option was gone, even if the money was still sitting with the insurer.

Insurers will also take reservations. A customer can book the conversion from one year before maturity, and it then happens automatically on the maturity date. Today, converting before maturity cancels the policy and builds the annuity from its surrender value, so anyone who wanted the full maturity payout as the base had to apply on the exact date.

Notices change too. The annual policy statement will explain the option, how to apply and the interest rate that applies, and insurers will send a reminder by mobile message one month before maturity.

Who can use it

Only policies with the annuity conversion rider qualify. The FSS counts about 2.02 million savings-type policies at the end of 2025, and 79.3% of them have it. Holders can check with their insurer. The announcement covers policies sold by life insurers.

There are conditions. Once the maturity payout has been collected, it cannot be converted. The age at which conversion is allowed and other terms differ by product. A sample notice attached to the announcement lists the insurer's mobile app, website and call center as the ways to apply. Insurers say they will explain who is covered and how to book on their websites and through call centers. The announcement does not say whether policies that matured before Dec. 1 are included.

What the annuity pays

The FSS gave an example: 100 million won ($74,400) converted by a 65-year-old man into a lifetime annuity at a declared interest rate of 2.5%. If he chooses a 10-year guarantee, meaning payments run for at least 10 years even if he dies sooner, he receives 388,510 won ($289) a month. With a 20-year guarantee it is 375,120 won ($279), and with a guarantee to age 100 it is 336,670 won ($251).

Buying a new annuity policy on the same terms would pay 378,090 won ($281) a month with the 10-year guarantee. Conversion pays 2.8% more, which works out to 10,420 won ($8) a month or 125,040 won ($93) a year. The FSS says the gap exists because a new policy carries sales and set-up charges and a conversion does not.

These are illustrations based on a 2.5% rate. Actual amounts depend on the product, the rate on the conversion date, and the holder's age and sex.

How long the man in the example has to live to break even

The FSS did not give a break-even age. We worked one out from its figures. At 388,510 won a month, total payments pass 100 million won after 258 months, or 21 years and 6 months. A man who starts at 65 gets there at 86 and a half. With the 20-year guarantee it takes 267 months, to age 87 and 3 months. With the guarantee to age 100 it takes 298 months, to age 89 and 10 months.

South Korea's 2024 life table puts life expectancy for a 65-year-old man at 19.5 more years, or age 84.5. In the same table, 46.7% of men alive at 65 reach 86, 41.8% reach 87 and 27.0% reach 90. With the 10-year or 20-year guarantee, the man in the example has to live two to three years longer than the average man of 65 before his payments exceed the 100 million won he handed over. With the guarantee to age 100, the break-even age of 89 years and 10 months falls inside the guaranteed period.

The life table reflects death rates for the whole population in 2024. It says nothing about one person's health or about future gains in longevity. The sum is also a simple one that ignores interest. A lump sum left in a bank deposit would earn interest, so measured against that the break-even age comes later still.

If he dies during the guarantee period, the payments for the remaining months are still made. Who receives them, and how, depends on the contract. Added up month by month, that floor is 46.62 million won ($34,700) with the 10-year guarantee and 90.03 million won ($67,000) with the 20-year one. Counting the 35 years from 65 to 100, it is 141.4 million won ($105,200) with the guarantee to age 100. That option pays out more than 100 million won however long he lives, but it pays 51,840 won ($39) a month less than the 10-year version.

Hard to undo

A lifetime annuity cannot, as a rule, be cancelled once payments begin. If a large medical or housing bill arrives, he may not be able to get the money out. Fixed-term annuities, and a type that pays out only the interest on the balance, may or may not allow cancellation depending on the contract.

The interest rate changes as well. After conversion the rider's declared rate applies, not the rate on the original savings policy, and the estimate given at the time of booking can shift with the rate and the balance on the conversion date.

Waiting can cost money. The FSS warns that the rate credited to an uncollected maturity payout can be lower than the rate during the policy term, and advises applying early. Converting outright before maturity, rather than booking, cancels the original policy, and its death benefit and other cover end.

The announcement does not say how conversion affects tax. That is a question to put to the insurer before signing.

What insurers get

The announcement frames the change as one of consumer choice and convenience. The announcement does not say what it means for insurers, but the mechanics are simple. When a maturity payout leaves as a lump sum, the insurer loses the money in one go. When it becomes an annuity, the money goes out over many years. The customer avoids the charges on a new annuity policy, and the insurer holds on longer to money that would otherwise leave at maturity.

So there are two comparisons to make: a lump sum against an annuity, and, for those who want an annuity, converting the existing policy against other annuity or pension products. The FSS itself tells customers to compare projected payments and payout terms before choosing.

What comes next

Life insurers are revising contract terms and procedures to start on Dec. 1, and each will explain booking and applications through its website and call center. The FSS says it will check that insurers follow through and track how much the option is used.

item.title: The Kospi is down 48% from its peak. Seoul is preparing its stabilization fund and easing buyback limits
item.description:
A 48% fall in five months

The Kospi closed at 4,708.54 on Monday, Nov. 23, down 3.31% on the day. That is 48.3% below its record close of 9,114.55 on June 22. The index is still 11.7% above where it ended 2025, at 4,214.17, which shows how far it had climbed in the first half.

Around 11:33 a.m. the index was down 5.11%, and the Korea Exchange suspended program trading for five minutes. Traders call this a sidecar: a short pause in computer-driven orders after a sharp drop in index futures. It also triggered on Friday, Nov. 20.

Chips and the won

Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are the two largest Kospi stocks, and their weight is why US-listed Korea funds such as the iShares MSCI South Korea ETF often trade with chip stocks. The government's joint release named the fall in US stocks as the reason for its emergency review.

The currency added to the loss for anyone counting in dollars. The Bank of Korea's closing rate moved from 1,330.8 won per dollar on Friday to 1,337.3 on Monday, a 0.5% weaker won.

What Seoul said it will do

On Sunday, Nov. 22, Finance Minister Lee Hyung-il met the governor of the Bank of Korea and the heads of the Financial Services Commission, which writes market rules, and the Financial Supervisory Service, which enforces them. Their joint release cited uncertainty around AI and chip companies' profits and funding, US data center rules, tighter chip export controls and US rate increases.

The officials also said medium- to long-term growth expectations for AI remain valid, and warned against excessive anxiety and panic selling. They then listed three steps from an existing contingency plan.

First, start preparing the Securities Market Stabilization Fund so it can be deployed whenever markets require it. Second, relax the daily limit on how many of their own shares listed companies can order, for three months from Nov. 24. Third, run a three-month special watch on illegal short selling by the regulator and the exchange, and monitor margin loans and forced selling by brokers.

The release does not give a size or a trigger for the fund. It says the work covers how the fund is activated and how to make it effective.

The buyback rule, in numbers

This is the step that takes effect first. Under the normal rule, a company buying back its own shares directly can order, each day, the larger of 10% of the shares it reported it would buy or 25% of its average daily volume over the month before the board decision. That figure can never exceed 1% of all its shares.

From Nov. 24 to Feb. 23, 2027, the daily cap is the full number of shares the company reported. Buybacks through a trust, where a company funds a trust that buys shares for it, were capped at 1% of shares a day and can now use the whole trust.

An example. A company with 100 million shares announces a buyback of 3 million. Under the old rule its daily cap could not go above 1 million, the 1% limit, so the buyback took at least three trading days. If its trading volume was thin, the cap fell as low as 300,000 a day, 10% of the plan, stretching the purchase over 10 days. Now it can place orders for all 3 million in one session.

The Financial Services Commission approved the change on Nov. 23. Korean company law still limits buybacks to profits available for dividends. The change raises a ceiling. It does not oblige any company to buy, and there is no evidence yet of its effect on prices.

What the fund looked like in 2020

The fund's 2020 design came on March 24 that year, during the pandemic sell-off. The release lists the five major financial holding companies and other leading firms, 18 financial companies in all, plus the exchange and related institutions, committing 10.7 trillion won, about $8.0 billion at today's rate. The firms would pay in when called, about 3 trillion won in the first round, and the fund would buy products that track the whole market, such as the Kospi 200, the index of the 200 largest listed stocks, rather than single stocks.

The Korea Herald and the Korea Times have both reported that the fund has not bought shares since 2008, so the 2020 money was never used. Neither the 2020 plan nor the 2026 release promises a level for the index.

What to watch next

Nov. 24 is the first day of the looser buyback rule. Companies must still announce buybacks before they place orders, so new filings on DART, Korea's corporate disclosure system, are the earliest sign of whether boards use it. The short-selling watch runs for three months. The ministers also said a capital market reform task force will be launched soon, and asked the National Assembly to pass pending tax and pension bills. No date was given for either, or for the fund.

item.title: South Korea to US West Coast container freight rates up 82% in October 2026, customs data show
item.description:
The question for anyone shipping Korean goods by sea

South Korea exported $77.4 billion of goods in the first 20 days of November, twice as much as a year earlier, the Korea Customs Service said on Nov. 23. As we reported earlier today, most of the gain is the price of chips, and the weight of Korea's exports this year is actually down 4.9%. Chips travel largely by air: airports handled 55.8% of Korea's export value over the past 12 months. So what does the headline mean for a US importer bringing in Korean cosmetics or machine parts by ship? The practical questions are whether space is tighter and whether the rate went up.

The release itself does not answer that. Two other government data sets do, through October: the average ocean freight that shippers declare on customs filings, by direction, rather than carrier tariffs or spot quotes, and the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries' count of containers by partner country.

Rates jumped on the US and Europe lanes, not the Asian ones

The average rate for a 40-foot container from Korea to the US West Coast was 82.3% higher in October 2026 than a year earlier, according to customs data. To the US East Coast it was up 84.9%, and to the EU 47.5%. In the same month the rate to China fell 6.3%, while Japan rose 2.9% and Vietnam 1.8%. The customs service does not publish the unit for these averages, so we report only percentage changes. Actual quotes vary by carrier and forwarder, and November is not in these data yet; weekly market indexes are the better guide to current quotes.

The turn has a clear date. From January to May, the West Coast rate averaged 15.5% less than a year earlier. Then it jumped 41.0% between May and June, and the June-October average ran 60.6% above the year before. The EU lane averaged 35.5% higher over the same five months.

More boxes on the same lanes

Loaded containers leaving Korean ports for the US, which excludes empties, were nearly flat from January to May (down 0.2%). From June to October they rose 17.2%, and October alone reached 249,000 TEU, up 37.7%. A TEU is one 20-foot container, and the US count covers both coasts. Loaded containers bound for EU member states rose 70.0% from June to October and 92.7% in October alone, after already running 13.9% higher in January to May.

Asia looks different. Over those five months, loaded boxes to China rose 2.4% and to Japan 1.6%, and to Vietnam they fell 3.1%. In October alone, boxes rose 9.7% to China, 7.3% to Japan and 12.5% to Vietnam, while rates on those lanes held near last year's level. Rate increases and box growth overlap on the US and EU lanes, though by very different margins. Neither agency explains the rise. Freight also depends on global vessel supply and fuel costs, so the data do not prove that Korean cargo pushed rates up.

One caution on Europe. The ministry counts containers leaving Korean ports by the country they are bound for, which can include other countries' cargo that changed ships in Busan. The ministry said Europe-related transshipment grew 108.4% in the third quarter, as our Nov. 20 piece on Busan and Incheon reported.

Export dollars and boxes moved apart

Do the math and the gap between dollars and boxes is wide. Korea's exports to China rose 145.6% in value in Nov. 1-20, while loaded containers to China were up 9.7% in October and the rate fell. Exports to the US rose 142.7% in value over the same 20 days. Loaded boxes to the US rose 37.7% in October.

The 20-day release does not split countries by product, so it cannot show how much of the US increase went by sea. Two things are clear. A doubling of export value in Nov. 1-20 is hard to read as a doubling of boxes going by sea; through October, loaded boxes to the US were up 38%. And rates to the US and Europe have been elevated since June, though these statistics alone cannot show how that relates to export value.

If you buy from Korea in the US or Europe

If you buy on CIF or CFR terms, the Korean seller books the freight and builds it into the quote. If you buy FOB and arrange your own ocean freight, you pay it directly. That does not mean your quote rose by the customs average, but contracts priced close to the spot market feel it most. The return leg is the opposite. The October rate from the US West Coast to Korea was 52.0% lower than a year earlier, about 24% of the rate in the other direction. Our Nov. 16 piece on backhaul freight goes into that imbalance.

What to watch next

Korea's trade ministry publishes full-month November trade by country on Dec. 1. The customs service's Dec. 1-10 figures come out at 9 a.m. Korea time on Dec. 11, which is 7 p.m. the evening before on the US East Coast. November freight and container figures will show up in the Korea Trade freight panel as soon as the two agencies update them. If US-lane rates ease while box counts hold, that would suggest box counts and rates do not always move together.

item.title: South Korea's imports jumped 39% in the first 20 days of November 2026. Chips and energy explain most of it
item.description:
$9.8 billion of a $14.2 billion increase

South Korea imported $50.3 billion of goods in the first 20 days of November, 39.4% more than a year earlier, the Korea Customs Service said on Nov. 23. That is $14.2 billion of extra buying. The period had 16 working days against 15.5 a year earlier, so the daily average rose about 35%. Exports doubled over the same period, as our earlier piece reported. This one looks only at what Korea bought.

Broken down by product, chips account for $4.7 billion, crude oil $3.1 billion, gas $1.2 billion and chipmaking equipment $0.8 billion. Together that is $9.8 billion, or 69% of the rise. The four items made up 41.8% of Korea's imports in those 20 days, up from 31.0% in the same period last year.

Everything else came to $29.3 billion, up 17.6%. Within that, imports of passenger cars rose 33.0%, machinery 13.8% and precision instruments 13.1%, while wireless devices fell 22.0%. Product names here follow the customs service's own grouping, so its chips line is broader than HS 8542, used below.

Less crude in October, at a higher price

Crude oil imports rose 83.4% by value in Nov. 1-20. The 20-day figures carry no volumes, and the nearest full month is October. In its October trade report, published Nov. 1, the trade ministry said the volume of crude imported that month fell 6.3% while the unit price rose 62.0%, lifting the bill 51.9%. Dubai crude, the benchmark for most of Korea's supply, averaged $110.73 a barrel in October against $65.00 a year earlier, up 70.4%. The ministry put the high price down to uncertain supply from the Middle East.

Customs data by HS code tell the same story over a longer stretch. In the 12 months to October 2026, crude imports (HS 2709) fell 3.7% in weight from the prior 12 months and rose 17.7% in value. The average tonne cost about $685, up from about $560.

The sources have shifted too. By weight over the same 12 months, crude from Saudi Arabia fell 15.6%, from Kuwait 27.2% and from Qatar 51.0%, while crude from the United Arab Emirates rose 4.5%. Crude from the United States rose 21.0%, taking its share of Korea's crude tonnage from 14.9% to 18.7%. Gas (HS 2711, which covers both LNG and LPG such as propane) moved the same way. Across all suppliers its weight fell 3.7% while its value rose 6.2%. Qatari gas fell 56.8% by weight, U.S. gas rose 14.2% and Canadian gas went from 0.76 million tonnes to 3.85 million. One caveat: in Nov. 1-20 alone, Korea's total imports from Saudi Arabia rose 148.7% by value. The release does not break that down by product, so it does not show whether volumes returned or the price did the work.

Chips cost 1.5 times as much for the same weight

Korea is one of the world's largest chip exporters and also a large buyer. Under the customs grouping, chip imports reached $9.3 billion in Nov. 1-20, up 103.4%.

Looking only at integrated circuits (HS 8542), imports in the 12 months to October were worth $93.0 billion, up 51.1%, while their weight slipped 0.3%. Korea paid about 1.5 times as much for nearly the same weight. China supplied 40.7% by value and Taiwan 35.4%. Memory chips from China fell 17.1% in weight and more than doubled in value, rising 118.6% to $33.4 billion. Weight is a rough measure for chips, and the data cannot distinguish a higher price for the same part from a shift to costlier parts.

Chipmaking equipment (HS 8486) is a different case. Imports rose 40.3% to $30.8 billion over the 12 months, and their weight rose 31.0%, so the increase is more than price. The Netherlands supplied 38.9% by value, Japan 21.3% and the United States 14.7%. Imports from the Netherlands rose 54.2%. The trade ministry counted $2.52 billion of chip equipment imports in October, up 49.2%, and the customs figure for Nov. 1-20 is up 48.6%.

If you sell to Korea

For sellers of consumer goods or general machinery, 17.6% is closer to their market than the 39.4% headline, though that remainder still includes refined petroleum (up 40.9%) and coal (up 31.8%). Even that is a figure in dollars, so higher prices are mixed in. In the 12-month data by HS code, imports outside the four items rose 13.5% in value and 1.2% in weight. The period and the classification differ from the 20-day release, so the two are not directly comparable.

By origin, imports in Nov. 1-20 rose 45.2% from the United States, 81.5% from Taiwan, 52.5% from China, 27.0% from Japan and 17.0% from the European Union, and fell 0.8% from Australia. The 20-day release does not split countries by product. Over the 12 months, Korea's imports of U.S. crude rose 44.3% by value and of U.S. gas 43.4%.

For chip equipment suppliers, the weight of Korea's imports rose 31.0% in the 12 months to October. Oil and gas sellers face a buyer that took 3.7% fewer tonnes of each over those 12 months and is shifting from Gulf suppliers toward North America.

What comes next

These are preliminary figures. Korea's customs service publishes early readings for the first 10 and 20 days of each month, and says some numbers may be revised until annual statistics are finalized in February 2027. The trade ministry is due to publish full-month November trade on Dec. 1, with crude volume and unit price and a split between energy and non-energy imports. The Dec. 1-10 customs figures are due Dec. 11.

item.title: South Korea's exports double in first 20 days of November 2026 on chips, yet this year's cargo weighs 4.9% less
item.description:
Exports double to $77.4 billion in Nov. 1-20

South Korea exported $77.4 billion of goods in the first 20 days of November, up 101.5% from the same period a year earlier, the Korea Customs Service said on Nov. 23. Imports rose 39.4% to $50.3 billion, leaving a surplus of $27.1 billion. The period had 16 working days, half a day more than last year, so customs also reports a daily average. Exports per working day came to $4.84 billion, up 95.2%.

Chips brought in $38.5 billion, up 294.4%, and made up 49.7% of the total. Without chips, exports came to $38.9 billion, up 35.8%, by our calculation. Refined petroleum rose 91.9% and computer peripherals 330.6%, while passenger cars fell 5.6%. Shipments to China rose 145.6%, to the United States 142.7%, to Taiwan 149.7%, to Vietnam 85.8% and to the European Union 25.7%.

That brings exports for the year to Nov. 20 to $1.0076 trillion. Customs put the moment the annual total first crossed $1 trillion at 2:09 p.m. Korean time on Nov. 19. The figures are preliminary and can be revised.

More dollars, fewer tonnes

A doubling in export value does not mean twice as much cargo is leaving Korean ports and airports. In a Nov. 20 release, the customs service said exports from Jan. 1 to Nov. 19 were worth $1.0015 trillion, up 62.9% from a year earlier, while their weight fell 4.9% to 166.57 million tonnes.

Divide one by the other and the average tonne of Korean exports was worth about $6,010 this year, against about $3,510 last year, a rise of 71%. The customs service attributes the fall in weight partly to a shift toward higher-value products. Under its own product classification, which is not the same as HS codes, chip exports rose 197.4% in value and 39.1% in weight.

Value for some goods, volume for others

The picture differs by product. We compared January to October with the same months of 2025, using customs data by HS code, the product numbering used in customs filings worldwide. Chips here means integrated circuits only (HS 8542), a narrower category than the customs classification above.

Integrated-circuit exports rose 170.3% to $303.1 billion, while their weight rose 7.1%. The whole $303.1 billion weighed 16,900 tonnes. Refined petroleum went the other way on weight, down 6.2%, yet its value rose 52.3% as the average value per kilogram climbed from $0.69 to $1.12. For both, value moved far more than weight.

Cosmetics and instant noodles are the opposite case. Cosmetics exports rose 30.7% in value and 25.4% in weight; ramen rose 25.8% and 21.8%. Their value per kilogram went up just 4.2% and 3.3%, so most of the growth is more product shipped. Steel and passenger cars moved less than 4% either way on both measures.

Why the central bank says October volume rose 43.9%

The Bank of Korea's trade indexes for October show export volume up 43.9% from a year earlier, which seems to contradict the falling tonnage. The two measure different things over different periods. The index covers October alone and leaves out ships and aircraft; the customs weight runs from Jan. 1 to Nov. 19. The bank derives volume by dividing export value by an export price index, and it notes that the index is not based on weight and includes changes in quality. Selling the same weight of a better-specified product can therefore show up as higher volume. Tonnage is what the cargo weighs.

So a higher value per kilogram does not mean the same product costs that much more. It mixes price increases with a shift to pricier products. On the central bank's October index, coal and petroleum products fell 3.5% in volume while rising 79.5% in value, the same direction as the January-October weight data.

If you buy from Korea, or move its cargo

For chips and fuel, the weight leaving Korea is close to last year's while the value is far higher. That reflects both higher prices and a richer product mix. Cosmetics and ramen are a different case. Value per kilogram is up only slightly, and the volume leaving Korea is up more than 20%.

For carriers and forwarders, record exports have not meant more tonnage. The weight leaving Korea is down, and the extra dollars are concentrated in chips, which weigh little for their value. More of the value is also leaving by air. By our calculation from customs data by port, 55.8% of Korea's export value left through airports in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 37.6% a year earlier.

When the next numbers land

A lighter total does not by itself mean factories produced less. These are 20-day preliminary figures, and the full month can look different. The trade ministry publishes November's full-month figures on Dec. 1. Customs releases Dec. 1-10 data on Dec. 11 at 9 a.m. Korean time, which is 7 p.m. the previous evening in New York. Weight and value per kilogram can be tracked in the monthly customs data by product, also on our Korea Trade pages.

item.title: South Korea plans a tool to find unclaimed medical insurance in 2027, but some claims will lapse first
item.description:
A trillion won waiting to be claimed

South Korea's Financial Services Commission (FSC) estimates that up to 1 trillion won ($750 million) in private medical insurance went unclaimed from 2024 to 2026, about 338.6 billion won ($254 million) of it in 2025 alone. It gave the figures at a Nov. 19 meeting on "silson" insurance (Korean for "actual loss"), the indemnity policies sold by private insurers that pay for what the national health insurance scheme leaves to patients.

The FSC's vice-chair said much of the money goes unclaimed because people cannot remember which clinic or pharmacy they visited, or because the bill is too small to justify getting the paperwork, photographing it and uploading it. It plans to add a finder tool to Silson24, the government-backed app that sends bills straight from hospitals and pharmacies to insurers. With the user's consent, the tool will pull card payment records through MyData, Korea's system that lets licensed firms gather a customer's financial records from banks and card companies, read off the clinic name, date and amount, and match those visits against the claims records of Korea Credit Information Services, the financial industry's central data agency. Visits with no matching claim will be flagged.

The launch is set only for "the first quarter of 2027". The Korea Insurance Development Institute, insurers, the data agency and MyData firms still have to build the system, and the relevant rules have to be amended.

When the three years start

Article 662 of the Commercial Act says a right to an insurance payout lapses if it is not exercised for three years. The limit was two years until an amendment took effect on March 12, 2015.

The statute does not say when the clock starts. In a July 13, 2023 ruling, the Supreme Court held that, absent special circumstances, it runs from the date of the insured event. Where the event could not objectively be confirmed, it runs from when the claimant knew or could have known of it. The FSC's announcement likewise says bills from the past three years can be claimed.

If the visit is taken as the insured event, counting starts the next day, so a visit on Dec. 15, 2023 can be claimed until Dec. 15, 2026. Under the Civil Act, a deadline that falls on a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday rolls over to the following day. Because Nov. 21 and 22, 2026 fall on a weekend, visits on Nov. 21 and 22, 2023 can still be claimed until Monday, Nov. 23. Claiming early is safer than counting on the rollover.

The gap before launch

If the tool goes live on March 31, 2027, it can reach visits from March 31, 2024 onward. Visits from Nov. 21, 2023 to March 30, 2024, a little over four months that can still be claimed today, will have lapsed by then.

Even a launch on Jan. 4, 2027, the first weekday of the quarter, would come too late for visits in 2023. Because the 1 trillion won estimate covers 2024 to 2026, visits from November and December 2023 are not counted in it at all.

Anyone with a silson policy who saw a doctor or filled a prescription in that window can look up the dates now rather than wait. Payouts are net of a deductible set by each policy, so a small pharmacy bill may return little or nothing.

How to find the dates now

The National Health Insurance Service website has a section called Geongang Moa ("health, gathered"), under My Health Management and then My Medical Use, that lists hospital, clinic and pharmacy visits from the past five years, with dates, prescriptions and days of medication. A separate treatment page on the same site covers only the last 12 months, so visits from late 2023 have to be found in Geongang Moa.

The 12-month page notes that recent visits show up only after two to three months, and that visits the provider has not billed to the national scheme may not appear. Card statements fill the gap, though how far back a card app goes varies by issuer and cash payments do not show up. The FSC's tool relies on the same card records, so it is likely to miss cash-paid visits too.

Once the dates are in hand, past claims can be checked in each insurer's app or with its call center, and Naeboheom Chajajum (cont.insure.or.kr), the industry's policy lookup site, shows which insurer holds a person's silson policy. Bills from providers linked to Silson24 can be claimed in the app; others need paper forms from the provider. As of Nov. 18, 57,258 providers, 54.2% of about 105,600, were linked.

Whose money moves

An unclaimed payout is money the insurer never paid. Whatever share policyholders do claim becomes payouts insurers had not been making, adding to their claim costs. The 1 trillion won is an upper estimate, so how much will actually be claimed is unknown.

Data firms sit in the middle. Card records come through MyData providers and claims records through the data agency. The FSC says it will set up clear consent steps and security first because the tool handles visit dates, claims history and payment data.

What comes next

Separately from the finder tool, since Oct. 7 Silson24 claims can be completed inside Naver Map, Naver Pay and Toss, some of the country's most-used map and payment apps. Silson24 has about 5.96 million registered users and has handled about 19.55 million claims so far, and the government aims to link 80% to 90% of providers by the end of 2026. Other silson measures from the same meeting, including discounts for switching to newer policies, were covered in a Nov. 20 article.

The finder tool is due in the first quarter of 2027. No exact date or rule-change timetable has been published.

item.title: Why 15 hours a week matters so much for part-time workers in South Korea
item.description:
Who the law covers

In October 2026, 1.819 million people in South Korea worked fewer than 15 hours a week, about six in every 100 employed, according to the monthly labor force survey, which counts hours actually worked and includes the self-employed. Ten years earlier, in October 2016, the figure was 898,000.

Korean law draws a line at those 15 hours. The Labor Standards Act, the country's main employment law, calls anyone who works shorter hours than a regular employee at the same workplace a part-time worker, and says their conditions should be set in proportion to their hours. But if contracted hours average under 15 a week over four weeks, two entitlements drop away: the paid weekly rest day and annual paid leave. The paid rest day means one extra day's wages each week on top of the hours worked, money Koreans call weekly holiday pay. A separate law excludes the same people from severance pay, which in Korea is owed to anyone leaving a job after a year or more, whatever the reason, at about a month's wages for each year worked. Such workers are known as ultra-short-time workers.

The 15 hours are not hours actually worked. They are the hours agreed in the contract. If the hours vary from week to week, the average over four weeks counts, or over the whole period if the job has lasted less than four weeks.

Some protections apply whatever the hours. Short hours do not take anyone out of the minimum wage or workplace-injury insurance. The duty to hand over a written contract also stands.

The rules described here are those in force in November 2026.

How the rules changed

When the Labor Standards Act was rewritten on March 13, 1997, it contained no 15-hour figure. It said only that parts of the law need not apply to part-timers whose hours were markedly short, and left the definition to a presidential decree. The wording about a four-week average under 15 hours a week entered the Act itself in an amendment of March 21, 2008, in force from July 1 that year.

From January 1, 2019, a decree under the Minimum Wage Act has counted paid rest hours when checking whether monthly pay meets the minimum. That is why a full-time month is counted as 209 hours: 40 hours of work plus eight paid rest hours a week, times the 4.345 weeks in an average month.

On August 14, 2025, the Supreme Court settled how to calculate weekly holiday pay for people who work fewer than five days a week. It is easy to assume that two eight-hour days earn eight hours of holiday pay. Under that ruling it is less.

The biggest change is to employment insurance, which pays unemployment benefits. Today a worker contracted for under 60 hours a month, or under 15 a week, is not covered, unless they work at the same place for three months or more or are a day laborer. An amendment promulgated on March 17, 2026, replaces the hours test with a pay test from January 1, 2027. A draft decree the Ministry of Employment and Labor published on July 10, 2026, sets the line at 800,000 won a month, about $600. At the 2027 minimum wage of 10,700 won an hour, 14 hours a week comes to about 650,000 won a month, short of that line at a single job, though anyone who stays three months or more is covered as now. The amended law also lets someone below the line at each job apply to join if pay from several workplaces together clears it; under the draft, that combined line would be 800,000 won too.

One hour, four hours' pay

A single hour changes a lot. The 2026 minimum wage is 10,320 won an hour, about $7.75 at 1,331 won to the dollar. A contract for 14 hours a week pays 144,480 won, about $109. A contract for 15 hours pays 154,800 won for the work plus 30,960 won in weekly holiday pay, or 185,760 won, about $140.

For the employer, the 15th hour costs 41,280 won, four times the hourly wage. After a year, severance pay is owed as well, and a business with five or more staff must also grant annual leave.

So an employer can hire two people for 14 hours each in place of one person for 28, an arrangement known as split contracts. A worker can put in 28 hours a week across two jobs and still get no holiday pay or severance from either, because each workplace is assessed separately.

Most people working such short hours are women. Of the 1.819 million people who worked under 15 hours a week in October 2026, 1.224 million, or 67%, were women. As noted, the survey counts hours actually worked, so it is not a count of ultra-short-time workers as the law defines them.

Where views differ

Should the 15-hour line stay? There are two camps.

One says it is needed. Very short jobs are mostly temporary, the argument runs, and holiday pay and severance reward steady service to one workplace. Requiring them for every worker would raise employers' costs and could make jobs worse.

The other says the line should go and the entitlements be paid in proportion to hours. That way an employer's cost rises only in step with the hours. This side also points out that contracted hours are in practice set by the employer, so a test based on them cannot stop split contracts.

The system itself now points two ways. Employment insurance drops the hours line in 2027 for a pay test, while the 15-hour line for the weekly rest day, annual leave and severance stays where it is.

What the courts decided

The two views met at the Constitutional Court, which rules on whether laws are constitutional. On November 25, 2021, it upheld the provision that excludes ultra-short-time workers from severance pay. Such work is generally temporary, the majority said, and does not fit a scheme premised on contribution to a workplace. Three justices dissented, arguing that severance is deferred wages and could simply be paid in proportion to hours.

What counts toward the 15 hours came before the Supreme Court, the top court for ordinary cases, on July 11, 2024. Part-time lecturers at a national university, each teaching 12 hours a week or less, had sued for weekly holiday pay and pay for unused annual leave. The appeals court treated the teaching hours in the contract as the contracted hours, and said the total stayed under 15 even with preparation time. The Supreme Court overturned that and sent the case back. Preparing classes, advising students, and setting and marking exams come with the job, it said, and that time has to be counted. Three times the teaching hours, the court added, can serve as a rough guide.

How many hours of holiday pay are owed was settled on August 14, 2025, in a case brought by taxi drivers working alternate days. For anyone working fewer than five days a week, the court said, the week should be treated as five working days unless the parties have agreed otherwise, and holiday pay should cover weekly contracted hours divided by five. Paying a full day's hours would give someone who works two days the same holiday pay as someone who works five, the court reasoned. Case law can change.

Where that leaves us

Start with the contracted hours written in the employment contract. If they average 15 or more a week over four weeks, and the worker turned up on every scheduled day that week, weekly holiday pay is owed. That holds even at businesses with four or fewer staff. Annual leave applies only where there are five or more.

Anyone contracted for 15 hours or more who stays a year or more is also owed severance, whatever the size of the business.

If the contract and the reality differ, the contract is not the last word. As in the 2024 ruling, courts ask how much time the job ordinarily takes. Rosters and clock-in records can serve as evidence, as can messages giving instructions.

Social insurance has its own tests. Enrollment in the national pension and health insurance through an employer generally turns on 60 contracted hours a month. Employment insurance uses the same hours line through 2026 and switches to pay in 2027. Either way, day laborers and anyone who works at the same place for three months or more are covered even below the line.

Unpaid weekly holiday pay counts as wages, and the right to claim it lapses after three years. It can be pursued through a complaint to a regional labor office or in court.

Do the math

Weekly holiday pay is weekly contracted hours divided by five, times the hourly wage. The formula fits anyone contracted for 15 to 40 hours over five days or fewer a week; at 40 hours it comes to eight hours' pay.

Take someone on 10,320 won an hour working five hours a day, five days a week, 25 hours in all. Holiday pay is five hours' worth, 51,600 won. Added to 258,000 won for the work, the week pays 309,600 won, about $233.

Take someone working two eight-hour days, 16 hours a week. Holiday pay is 16 divided by 5, or 3.2 hours' worth: 33,024 won, about $25.

The 2027 minimum wage is 10,700 won an hour. At 15 hours a week, holiday pay will be 32,100 won. Try your own hours and wage in the calculator below.

If you run a business

You must hand over a written contract stating pay and contracted hours. Failing to do so can bring a fine of up to 5 million won, about $3,760. A business with five or more staff that hires a part-timer must also put the working days and the hours for each day in writing, or face an administrative penalty of up to 5 million won.

Not giving a paid weekly rest day to someone contracted for 15 hours or more is punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine of up to 20 million won, about $15,000.

At a business with five or more staff, a part-timer can be asked to work beyond the contracted hours only with their consent, and by no more than 12 hours a week. Those extra hours must be paid at a premium of at least 50% of the ordinary wage. Imposing them without consent can bring a fine of up to 10 million won, about $7,500.

From January 1, 2027, employment insurance moves to a pay test. Under the draft decree, the once-a-year report of total pay would be abolished, and monthly pay would have to be reported by the end of the month after it is paid.

item.title: South Korea now imports more cars from China than from Germany by value, and 92% of those from China are electric
item.description:
Which factories supply South Korea's imported cars

A badge tells you who owns the brand. A customs declaration records where the car was built. Counted by country of origin, China has narrowly become the largest source, by value, of the passenger cars South Korea imports. Of the $12.74 billion in cars that cleared Korean customs in January–October 2026, $4.22 billion came from plants in China and $4.19 billion from Germany, according to our calculation from data published by the Korea Customs Service, the government's customs agency. The figures cover HS heading 8703, the customs code for passenger cars.

A year earlier the order was reversed and the gap was wide: $4.41 billion from Germany and $2.24 billion from China. Imports from China rose 88.3% while those from Germany fell 5.0%. China's share of import value went from 20.3% to 33.1%, and Germany's from 40.0% to 32.9%. The lead is about $23 million, and it changes hands month to month. China was ahead in five of the ten months this year and Germany in the other five.

Almost all of the growth is electric

Battery electric cars made up 92.0% of the value imported from China, or $3.88 billion, up 99.2% from a year earlier. South Korea's electric car imports from all countries rose from $2.73 billion to $5.09 billion, and Chinese plants supplied 76.1% of that. Electric cars now account for 40.0% of the value of all passenger cars Korea imports.

Germany's mix looks different. Hybrids, including plug-ins, were worth $2.16 billion, more than half of the German total, and fell 11.2%. German-built electric cars rose 9.4% to $720 million.

Prices differ too. Dividing import value by weight for electric cars only, those from China averaged $15.0 a kilogram, against $20.4 from Germany and $31.0 from the United States. For a car weighing 2 tonnes that works out to roughly $30,000, $41,000 and $62,000. These are declared import values, before duty, tax and dealer margin, and they are not a like-for-like comparison, because each country ships a different set of models. The US figure rests on a small volume and moves a lot from year to year.

Which brands are behind the numbers

Customs data record the country where a car was built, not its brand. Registration data fill in the brands. They count vehicles registered rather than import value, so they cannot be set directly against the customs figures above.

South Korea registered 310,846 new imported passenger cars in January–October 2026, according to the Korea Automobile Importers & Distributors Association, an industry group. Tesla, the US company, led with 98,313, followed by Germany's BMW with 63,562 and Mercedes-Benz with 49,993, China's BYD with 21,731 and Japan's Lexus with 12,543. By model, the Tesla Model Y was first with 78,631, ahead of the Mercedes-Benz E-Class at 21,034, the BMW 5 Series at 18,917 and the Tesla Model 3 at 15,459.

A US brand accounts for much of the rise in cars from China. Of the imported vehicles registered in the first half of 2026, 79,444, or 41.2%, were built in China and 57,954, or 30.1%, in Germany, South Korean media reported, citing the Korea Automobile & Mobility Association, the carmakers' lobby. The Model Y and Model 3 that Tesla builds in Shanghai drove the increase. BYD's Sealion 7 and Dolphin also grew, as did the Polestar 4, a Swedish-brand car built in China. Zeekr, another Chinese brand, has started selling in South Korea and registered 129 cars in October.

Cars counted as German come mainly from German brands' plants in Germany. BMW builds the 5 Series in Dingolfing and Mercedes-Benz builds the E-Class in Sindelfingen.

The Korea–China trade deal left cars out

South Korea's base tariff on passenger cars is 8%. Under the Korea–US free trade agreement, in force since 2012, Korea halved the rate for US-built cars to 4% at once and agreed to remove it in the fifth year. The European Union says the remaining duties under its agreement with Korea were removed by July 1, 2016, apart from a few farm products. That agreement covers cars built in Germany. China is the exception. The Korea–China free trade agreement, in force since 2015, excluded cars from tariff cuts on both sides.

Seoul explained the exclusion at the time. A November 2014 briefing document from South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, as it was then called, said the decision reflected Korean carmakers' strategy of building in China and domestic concern about a surge in imports of foreign-brand cars made in China. The ministry said Beijing had also refused to open its own car market, despite repeated Korean requests.

Twelve years after that briefing, with cars still outside the agreement's tariff cuts, China was the largest source of Korea's car imports by value in the first ten months of 2026. Customs data do not show how many of those cars carry foreign badges.

The follow-up talks that the two governments declared substantially concluded on November 18 cover services and investment.

US-built cars: fewer petrol models, more EVs

Imports of cars built in the United States fell 4.8% to $1.81 billion, but the mix shifted. Petrol and diesel cars fell 33.2% and hybrids 14.1%, while electric cars rose 5.5-fold, from $60 million to $330 million. The trade data do not say why. Some of the US-built cars carry German badges. BMW assembles SUVs such as the X3 and X5 in South Carolina, and cars shipped from a US plant are recorded as American. Imports of cars built in Japan fell 8.8% to $590 million.

South Korea sells few cars to China

Trade in the other direction is small. South Korea exported $160 million of passenger cars to China over the same ten months, down 36.6% from $250 million. Imports were 26 times exports, leaving a deficit of $4.06 billion in passenger cars alone.

South Korean media reported on November 22, citing the Korea International Trade Association, a business group, and the trade ministry, that the country's car trade deficit with China reached $4.23 billion in January–October, about 6 trillion won and a record. The reports pointed to cars from the Shanghai plant of Tesla, the US electric car maker, and to BYD, the Chinese electric car maker. Customs data do not identify brands, so the split between companies cannot be checked from this source. The reported figure may cover a wider range of vehicles than ours. Our $4.06 billion counts passenger cars only.

For anyone selling cars into South Korea, the part of the import market that is growing is electric, and about three-quarters of that value comes from plants in China, which get no tariff cut under the Korea–China agreement.

How to read these numbers

Country here means where the car was built, not where the brand is based. The figures are values declared at customs in US dollars, not unit sales. They cover passenger cars only and leave out buses and trucks. Value per kilogram compares countries that ship different models, so it should not be read as the price gap for the same car. Recent months may be revised, and with China and Germany only 0.2 percentage points apart in share, the order could change.

item.title: Marginal vs average tax rate: what crossing a South Korean tax bracket costs
item.description:
The margin

In economics, the margin means one more unit at the edge: one more hour of work, one more helping, one more hire. Most real choices are not all or nothing but a little more or a little less, so the useful question is what that one extra unit gains and what it costs.

Think of an all-you-can-eat buffet. Once you have paid the 29,000 won, about $22, the price has nothing to do with whether you go back for a third plate. You weigh the pleasure of that plate against feeling too full. The money is gone whichever way you decide.

Taxes are one of the places this way of thinking matters most. South Korea's income tax is progressive, so the share of income you pay on average and the extra tax on the next won you earn are two different numbers. Confuse them and you will misjudge what a raise is worth.

New brackets from 2023

On December 31, 2022, South Korea amended its Income Tax Act and moved the bracket thresholds from 2023. The bottom bracket, taxed at 6%, was widened from taxable income of 12 million won or less to 14 million won or less, about $10,500. The 15% bracket, which had covered 12 million to 46 million won, now runs from 14 million to 50 million won, about $37,600. The amendment said the aim was to lighten the tax burden on low and middle earners.

The 24% bracket now starts at 50 million won instead of 46 million and still ends at 88 million. Above that nothing changed: 35% up to 150 million won, then 38%, 40% and 42%, and 45% on anything above 1 billion won. The same table applies in 2026.

Taxable income is not salary. It is what remains after the deductions set by law, and it is the amount the rates are applied to. Later we will work out how far apart the two can be.

Earning 1 million won more

On taxable income of exactly 50 million won, the rate table gives 6.24 million won of national income tax, about $4,700, before any tax credits. That is 6% on the first 14 million won plus 15% on the next 36 million. As a share of the whole, the average tax rate, it is 12.5%.

If that person earns 1 million won more, about $750, taxable income reaches 51 million won and enters the 24% bracket. But the 24% does not apply to all 51 million. It applies only to the 1 million won above the threshold, so the tax rises by 240,000 won, about $180, to 6.48 million. The average rate edges up to 12.7%.

If the whole 51 million were taxed at 24%, the bill would be 12.24 million won. The common fear that crossing a bracket raises the tax on everything you earn comes from confusing those two calculations. In reality, earning an extra 1 million won still leaves 760,000 won in your pocket. Korea also levies a local income tax equal to a tenth of the national tax, 24,000 won here, and even with that included you keep 736,000 won, about $550.

That 24% on the next won is the marginal tax rate. When you decide whether to work extra hours or take on side income, the number that matters is the marginal rate, not the average.

Which bracket is a 50 million won salary in?

It is easy to assume that a salary of 50 million won puts you right at the edge of the 24% bracket. Run it through the law and it does not.

Korean employees first get an earned income deduction, an allowance every wage earner receives automatically that grows with pay. For total pay between 45 million and 100 million won, it is 12 million won plus 5% of the pay above 45 million. On a 50 million won salary that removes 12.25 million won, leaving 37.75 million. Subtract the basic personal deduction of 1.5 million won and taxable income is 36.25 million won, about $27,200. Even before pension contributions or any other deduction, that is the 15% bracket.

The marginal rate can be worked out too. In this pay range, each extra 10,000 won of salary raises the earned income deduction by 500 won, so taxable income goes up by only 9,500 won. At 15% that is 1,425 won of national income tax per 10,000 won earned, or about 1,570 won with local income tax, before the pension and health insurance deductions that shrink it slightly. The final bill is lower still after tax credits, such as a credit every employee gets on wage income (not the same as America's EITC). Employers withhold tax each month and settle the exact amount early the next year in what Koreans call the year-end settlement, so treat these figures as a guide to your bracket, not a forecast of your bill.

A tax cut that left most marginal rates alone

Thinking at the margin also changes how the 2023 reform looks. Redo the tax at each level of taxable income under the old and new tables. Anyone at 12 million won or less saw no change. From 14 million to 46 million won, the tax worked out from the rate table fell by 180,000 won, about $135, and at 50 million won or more it fell by 540,000 won, about $406. These figures are before tax credits; for lower earners, whose credit is a share of their tax, the actual saving was smaller.

Yet on the rate table, the rate on the next won changed in only two ranges. Between 12 million and 14 million won it fell from 15% to 6%, and between 46 million and 50 million won it fell from 24% to 15%. A person with taxable income of 30 million won pays 180,000 won less, but each extra won is still taxed at 15%, as before. Someone at 100 million won saves 540,000 won, and their marginal rate is still 35%. The same law also trimmed the wage earner's tax credit at the top. For employees whose total pay is above 120 million won, about $90,000, the cap on that credit starts at 500,000 won and shrinks by 50 won for every 100 won of pay above that line, down to a floor of 200,000 won. Before 2023 it stayed at 500,000 won. From 120.6 million won of pay, the cap is 300,000 won lower than before the reform, so a cut worth 540,000 won on the rate table is really 240,000 won, about $180. In the 600,000 won stretch in between, every extra 10,000 won of pay cuts the credit by 5,000 won, so the burden on the next won actually rose.

For anyone outside those two ranges, the reform cut the tax bill by a set amount without changing the rate on the next won. Everyone above 12 million won of taxable income paid less on the rate table, but only those in two narrow ranges saw that rate fall, and for a sliver of top earners the burden on the next won rose. How people actually changed their work cannot be read from the rate table alone. When a tax cut or rise is in the news, it helps to ask two separate questions. How much less will people pay, and has the rate on the next won changed?

When the average is the right number

The margin is not always the right lens. To work out how much tax you will pay next year in total, and so how to plan the household budget, you need the average rate. Someone with taxable income of 51 million won who sets aside 24% because that is their bracket would budget 12.24 million won, nearly twice the actual 6.48 million.

A small shop works the same way. Whether to serve one more customer depends on what that customer pays and what the ingredients cost. Whether to keep the shop open at all depends on total sales against total costs, rent included. Use the margin to decide whether to do a bit more, and the totals to decide whether to do it at all.

The rate table has no cliffs, but rules that switch on at an income threshold do. Article 50 of the Income Tax Act lets a taxpayer claim an extra 1.5 million won basic deduction for a spouse whose income, after the law's own deductions, is 1 million won or less, about $750. A spouse with only a salary qualifies up to 5 million won of pay, about $3,750. One won past that line and the taxpayer loses the whole deduction: in the 15% bracket, about 247,500 won of extra tax, local tax included, for a single won of the spouse's income. That is the law as of November 2026; the government's August 2026 tax plan would raise the line to 3 million won of income (7.5 million won of pay for salary-only earners), if the National Assembly passes it.

Using it when you read the news

When a news story gives you a number, ask whether it describes the whole or only the last unit. A phrase like 'a 24% tax bracket' sounds like a share of everything you earn, but it applies only to the slice above the threshold.

The next chapter is about incentives. Just as the marginal rate can change whether people work more or less, people change what they do when prices and rules change, and the results do not always match what policymakers expected.

item.title: The Big Mac index 2026 puts Pakistan and South Korea at almost the same price
item.description:
Five cents apart
